  Dude 😄 — this website looks insanely technical, but the basic idea is much   
  simpler.                                                                      
                                                                                
  Think of Bitcoin as a giant public notebook that nobody can secretly erase or 
  change.                                                                       
                                                                                
  Normally, that notebook keeps track of BTC. The people behind crc.garden are  
  trying to use that same Bitcoin notebook to also keep track of another thing  
  called LEAF. LEAF is not Bitcoin. It is a separate token whose rules are      
  called CRC-20 on this project. The site describes the current system as       
  “client validated,” meaning special software reads Bitcoin transactions and   
  figures out who owns how much LEAF.                                           
                                                                                
  Here is the easiest way to understand the website:                            
                                                                                
  🌱 LEAF = the token they created.                                             
  CRC-20 = the rulebook that says how LEAF can be created and moved.            
  Bitcoin = the big notebook where the important transaction evidence is        
  written.                                                                      
  Mint = create/get new LEAF according to the rules.                            
  Transfer = send LEAF from one Bitcoin address to another.                     
  Activity = a public history showing these actions.                            
  Wallet = where you connect your Bitcoin wallet and see BTC, ORDI, and LEAF.   
  Market = where they intend people to buy/sell LEAF.                           
  So what actually happens?                                                     
  Imagine you and I have Bitcoin wallets.                                       
                                                                                
  I do a special Bitcoin transaction that basically contains enough information 
  for the CRC-20 software to understand:                                        
                                                                                
  “Bob now owns 100,000 LEAF.”                                                  
                                                                                
  Bitcoin itself mainly sees a Bitcoin transaction.                             
                                                                                
  The CRC-20 software sees the Bitcoin transaction plus the special CRC-20      
  rules, and says:                                                              
                                                                                
  “Okay, according to our rulebook, Bob owns 100,000 LEAF.”                     
                                                                                
  That's an important difference. Bitcoin nodes do not treat LEAF like BTC.     
  LEAF is another system using Bitcoin transactions as its foundation/record.   
  The site's own timeline describes the present PRECOP → LEAF stage as client   
  validated and talks about an intended move “from an overlay toward covenant   
  execution.”                                                                   
                                                                                
  Why are they doing this?                                                      
  They want to build things people normally associate with Ethereum-style DeFi  
  — tokens, trading, loans, stablecoins, etc. — while using Bitcoin L1 as the   
  base ledger.                                                                  
                                                                                
  Their underlying project is called PRECOP. Its repository says the goal is    
  financial applications such as decentralized exchanges and collateralized     
  loans using Bitcoin's UTXO system, without requiring a Bitcoin soft fork.     
                                                                                
  The fancy words on the homepage — Taproot, UTXO

   crc = new CRC20()                                                            
                                                                                
  await crc.balance(address)

  The protocol people may have low-level implementations, but developer

  Stripe didn't invent payments.                                                
  They made payments pleasant for developers.

  4. Something much more fun: LEAF apps                                         
                                                                                
  This direction may actually be better than infrastructure if your goal is     
  “cool + viral + make money.”                                                  
                                                                                
  Don't build about LEAF.                                                       
                                                                                
  Build something where LEAF is used.                                           
                                                                                
  For example:                                                                  
                                                                                
  🌱 LEAF Poker / Prediction game                                               
  🌱 LEAF tipping bot                                                           
  🌱 LEAF paid chat                                                             
  🌱 LEAF faucet/game                                                           
  🌱 LEAF raffle                                                                
  🌱 LEAF token-gated community                                                 
  🌱 LEAF marketplace                                                           
  🌱 LEAF paywall                                                               
  🌱 LEAF quests/rewards                                                        
  That pushes the ecosystem forward because suddenly LEAF has somewhere to go,  
  rather than everyone just staring at their balance.                           
                                                                                
  There's a key distinction:                                                    
                                                                                
  CRC Garden currently answers:                                                 
                                                                                
  “How do I get / hold / transfer / trade LEAF?”                                
                                                                                
  You could                                                                     
                                                                                
  What does telegram bot do ?                                                   
  The Telegram bot would be like a little CRC/LEAF assistant inside Telegram.   
                                                                                
  You send it a wallet address, and it replies with useful info without making  
  you open the website.                                                         
                                                                                
  For example:                                                                  
                                                                                
  /wallet bc1p... → shows that wallet’s LEAF balance and recent transfers.      
  /watch bc1p... → watches that wallet and messages you when it sends or        
  receives LEAF.                                                                
  /whales → shows the biggest recent LEAF transfers.                            
  /holders → shows large LEAF holders.                                          
  /stats → shows network activity, transfers, active wallets, etc.              
  /alert 1000000 → tells you whenever someone moves more than 1,000,000 LEAF.   
  The most useful part is alerts.                                               
                                                                                
  Instead of checking CRC Garden all day, Telegram could message you:           
                                                                                
  🌱 Large LEAF transfer                                                        
  2,400,000 LEAF moved                                                          
  From: bc1p...abc                                                              
  To: bc1p...xyz                                                                
  30 seconds ago                                                                
                                                                                
  So the bot is basically:                                                      
                                                                                
  CRC Garden data + notifications + very fast commands                          
                                                                                
  And the business model could be simple: free users watch 1–3 wallets, while   
  paid users get more watched wallets, whale alerts, faster notifications,      
  custom thresholds, and maybe API access.                                      
                                                                                
  The bot itself could probably be the fastest useful product to build around   
  CRC-20, because you don’t need to build a full dashboard first.

  Bitcoin does not enforce Cove. Only your indexer does.

  - A mint of 900,000,000 tokens
  - A mint that pays 1 sat
  - A transfer of tokens you never owned

  Your spec is good. One note on item 1.

  ▎ H, treasuryScript, and settlementScript become immutable literal protocol 
  ▎ constants... Runtime env may verify them but must not define consensus 
  ▎ configuration.

  This is the right call and it is the most important item in your list.
  Consensus values in env means two indexers with different .env files
  silently disagree and both think they are right. Putting them in a committed
  constant makes disagreement loud instead of silent.

  Make sure the env check fails the process on mismatch, not just logs.
  "Verify" must mean "refuse to run", or it is decoration.

  One warning on item 4

  ▎ Restart bitcoind with mempool persistence disabled/cleared after 
  ▎ invalidation

  That will work. But it makes the test prove something weaker than it looks.

  If you clear the mempool, you prove "a TRANSFER that was never re-broadcast 
  stays absent." Real reorgs do not clear mempools — the orphaned transaction
  sits there and gets re-mined within a block or two.

  Better: keep the mempool, and assert the stronger property — that even if
  TRANSFER is re-mined on the new branch, your final state root still equals a
  clean replay of the real chain. That is what actually happens in
  production.

  Use the mempool clear only if the stronger version proves impossible in CI.
  Either way, say in the test comment which one you proved.

⏺ Second audit back. Your item 4 instinct was right — and there is a deeper
  problem underneath it.

  🔴 Your reorg test proves nothing

  regtest-reorg.ts:298 — the headline assertion:

  const recovered = new CoveIndexer(CFG);
  await indexAndPersist(provider, store, recovered, genesis, newTip);
  const recoveredRoot = recovered.getStateRoot();   // ← from MEMORY

  const clean = new CoveIndexer(CFG);
  await indexRange(provider, clean, genesis, newTip);
  const cleanRoot = clean.getStateRoot();            // ← from MEMORY

  assert(recoveredRoot === cleanRoot);

  Both roots come from the same code folding the same blocks. Postgres is
  written and never read back.

  This can only fail if bitcoind returns different bytes twice. It is a
  determinism check wearing a reorg-test label.

  A bug that completely broke reorg recovery would leave this test green.

  The fix is one line of intent: read recoveredRoot out of Postgres, not out
  of the indexer.

  You also correctly spotted the mempool re-mining issue in item 4. Keep that
  — but it is the second problem, not the first.

  🔴 There is no reorg recovery to test

  cli.ts:259 — the entire reorg response is:

  ▎ clear all Cove data → re-index from genesis

  No rollback. No common-ancestor walk. The canonical column exists on four
  tables and is only ever set true. Nothing ever marks a row false.

  Your mock chain worker already does this properly —
  apps/worker/src/sync.ts:37 walks back to the common ancestor and marks
  orphans. The new Cove store threw that away and started over.

  Worse: during the rebuild the database holds empty Cove state with no 
  in-progress flag. Anything reading balances sees zeros as truth.

  🔴 Esplora trusts whatever it is told

  You fixed this in the Core provider — provider.ts:120 checks the block hash
  and the merkle root.

  esplora.ts:93-101 got none of it. It asks for a block, accepts whatever txid
  list comes back, and folds it into your state root as canonical.

  And mainnet-canary.ts uses Esplora for block data and for the mainnet
  broadcast.

  Also: getBestHeight is parseInt with no NaN check. An HTML error page served
  with HTTP 200 → NaN → every loop indexes zero blocks → reports a clean
  empty state root as success.

  🔴 The worker will crash-loop on day one

  cli.ts:291 — the scan has no retry. One blip from the public RPC node kills
  the process. On restart it replays from genesis — tens of thousands of
  sequential calls to the same public node, which then rate-limits you. Crash.
  Repeat.

  And sync is quadratic: every block re-writes every event since genesis,
  every token, every balance, plus a full table scan of cove_balances. A
  30k-block backfill never finishes.

  🟠 Your item 3 is correct and urgent

  mutinynet-proof.ts:211 broadcasts, then writes the manifest. A 20-second
  timeout on an accepted transaction → no record → next run builds a different
  transaction spending the same input.

  That is a real double-spend window. Your "persist before broadcast" fix
  closes it.

  Related: decideNextAction returns a reason string saying "resolve before 
  re-broadcast" — and nothing reads it. Every caller branches on action only.
  The guard is a comment.

  🟠 Your CI does not gate anything

  cove-regtest.yml is the only workflow in the repo. It runs one command.

  Your 283 unit tests, lint, typecheck and build run in no CI job at all.

  ✅ Two things done right

  - regtest-reorg.ts:207 asserts chain === "regtest" before every mutating 
  call. Genuine runtime gate. Best network control in the new code.
  - The manifest holds no keys, is 0600, and is gitignored. Amounts are
  hardcoded constants, never read from the manifest — so a tampered manifest
  cannot change an amount.

❯ why cant we simulate some type of liquidity now?                            
  We absolutely can simulate liquidity now.                                   
                                                                              
  Think of it like this:                                                      
                                                                              
  You: “The curve sold out. What happens next?”                               
                                                                              
  Cove: “Okay, pretend we now have two buckets:”                              
                                                                              
  160,000,000 FROG                                                            
  +                                                                           
  0.24 BTC reserve                                                            
  Then we create a virtual pool in Cove’s test environment:                   
                                                                              
  FROG pool: 160M                                                             
  BTC pool:  0.24 BTC                                                         
  If someone buys FROG, they put BTC into the pool and get FROG out.          
                                                                              
  If someone sells FROG, they put FROG into the pool and get BTC out.         
                                                                              
  So:                                                                         
                                                                              
  BUY:                                                                        
  BTC → pool                                                                  
  FROG → buyer                                                                
                                                                              
  SELL:                                                                       
  FROG → pool                                                                 
  BTC → seller                                                                
  The price moves depending on how much FROG and BTC are left in the pool.    
                                                                              
  We can build and test this right now on regtest or Mutinynet.               
                                                                              
  The only reason I wouldn’t call it “real Cove liquidity” yet is because     
  Cove V1 currently has no Bitcoin-level rule saying:                         
                                                                              
  “These 160M tokens and this BTC must belong to this pool and must be traded 
  by these exact rules.”                                                      
                                                                              
  So we can simulate the whole experience now, prove the math, UX,            
  buying/selling, fees, slippage, graduation, etc.                            
                                                                              
  Then once we like how it works, we turn that simulation into an actual Cove 
  V2 liquidity protocol.                                                      
                                                                              
  The fastest path would be:                                                  
                                                                              
  DEPLOY                                                                      
  → people MINT                                                               
  → 840M sold                                                                 
  → GRADUATE                                                                  
  → create virtual 160M FROG / BTC pool                                       
  → BUY                                                                       
  → SELL                                                                      
  That would let us test the full launchpad story immediately without risking 
  real BTC while we decide the final on-chain rules.                          
                                                                              
  yeah lets just try to build this asap                                       
                                                                              
  Worked for 35s                                                              
                                                                              
  Yep. Fastest move: build the liquidity pool as a deterministic simulator    
  first, without changing Cove V1 mainnet rules yet.                          
                                                                              
  And the numbers actually line up nicely. If graduation uses the full curve  
  reserve:                                                                    
                                                                              
  160,000,000 reserved tokens                                                 
  24,196,788 sats collected by the curve                                      
  the starting pool price is about 151,230 sats per 1M tokens, while Cove's   
  final mint stage is 149,731 sats per 1M. So the handoff from minting →      
  trading is naturally very close in price.                                   
                                                                              
  Give the agent this:                                                        
                                                                              
  COVE — BUILD GRADUATION + VIRTUAL LIQUIDITY POOL ASAP                       
                                                                              
  Baseline: current main.                                                     
                                                                              
  Goal: build and demonstrate the complete product lifecycle:                 
                                                                              
  DEPLOY                                                                      
  → MINT through 840M public supply                                           
  → SOLD OUT                                                                  
  → GRADUATE                                                                  
  → seed virtual liquidity                                                    
  → BUY                                                                       
  → SELL                                                                      
  Important: this is a deterministic Cove liquidity simulator for             
  mock/regtest/testing. Do NOT change Cove V1 mainnet wire consensus or       
  activate this liquidity design on mainnet yet.                              
                                                                              
  Pool model                                                                  
  Use a simple constant-product AMM:                                          
                                                                              
  BTC reserve × token reserve = k                                             
  At graduation seed:                                                         
                                                                              
  tokenReserve = 160,000,000 tokens                                           
  btcReserve   = token.reserveSats

⏺ Read it. The spec is good. Your maths checks out. Three things to fix before
  they build.

  ✅ Your numbers are right

  I verified them:

  24,196,788 sats ÷ 160,000,000 tokens = 151,230 sats per 1M
  Final mint stage                     = 149,731 sats per 1M

  1.0% apart. The handoff from minting to trading is smooth. Nobody gets a
  price shock at graduation. That is a genuinely nice property and it fell out
  of your curve design by accident.

  🔴 One line in your spec is a real bug

  ▎ "k does not decrease with zero fees except integer rounding rules"

  Backwards. k must never decrease. Not even by rounding.

  If rounding ever favours the trader, someone runs ten thousand tiny trades
  and drains the pool one satoshi at a time. It is a known AMM attack.

  Change it to:

  ▎ Every rounding decision must favour the pool. Round token output down, 
  ▎ round sats output down, round pool input up. Test: k_after >= k_before 
  ▎ after every trade, always. Add a test that runs 10,000 dust trades and 
  ▎ asserts k only grows.

  🟠 Your pool is very thin

  At 0.242 BTC total, here is what trades do:

  ┌─────────────┬─────────────────┐
  │  Buy size   │   Price moves   │
  ├─────────────┼─────────────────┤
  │ 10,000 sats │ +0.01%          │
  ├─────────────┼─────────────────┤
  │ 0.01 BTC    │ +8%             │
  ├─────────────┼─────────────────┤
  │ 0.1 BTC     │ +100% — doubles │
  └─────────────┴─────────────────┘

  One person with 0.1 BTC doubles the price. That is not a bug in your design
  — it is what a 0.242 BTC raise produces.

  Not a reason to stop. But put price impact in the UI in red above 5%, and
  know that this market is small enough for one person to move alone.

  🟠 Three gaps in the spec

  1. Say what reserveSats excludes. Your 1% platform fee goes to the same
  settlement address as the curve money. Write it explicitly: "btcReserve =
  curve contributions only, NOT the 1% platform fee, NOT the 10,000 sat launch
  fee." Otherwise someone seeds the pool with your revenue.

  2. Add a minimum trade size. Dust trades plus rounding is where AMMs leak.
  Reject anything below, say, 1,000 sats.

  3. Say who can trade. Permissionless, or gated? It changes the design.
  Decide now, not later.

  ⚠️  The thing to keep saying out loud

  Your spec already says it, and it is the right call:

  ▎ "Do not claim reserve BTC is currently trustlessly pooled."

  Keep that. In the real version, that 0.242 BTC sits in your wallet. There is
  no Bitcoin rule forcing you to honour a sell. Users are trusting you, not
  the chain.

  Simulating it first is exactly right. You prove the mechanics without asking
  anyone to trust anything yet.

  Have the demo print a "what the platform holds" line at each step:

  Platform treasury:  251,968 sats  (launch fee + 1%)
  Pool BTC:        24,196,788 sats  (owed to holders)

  Because the moment this is real, that second number is a liability, not
  revenue. Seeing it in the transcript keeps that honest.

  What Cove actually uses

  P2WPKH (22 bytes) or P2TR (34 bytes)

  packages/protocol/src/cove/validator.ts:13

  Those are ordinary addresses. Plain wallets. No script conditions, no
  spending rules, no locks.
  
  Your treasury and settlement addresses are single-key wallets. On-chain they
  look exactly like anyone's personal wallet.
  
  Cove's rules live in your indexer, not in Bitcoin script.

  The harder news

  As of my knowledge, there are no general covenants on Bitcoin mainnet. None.

  Every one is still a proposal:

  ┌────────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │          Proposal          │                  Status                  │
  ├────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ CTV (BIP-119)              │ Not activated                            │
  ├────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ OP_CAT (BIP-347)           │ Disabled since 2010. Re-enabling is a    │
  │                            │ proposal.                                │
  ├────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ SIGHASH_ANYPREVOUT         │ Not activated                            │
  │ (BIP-118)                  │                                          │
  ├────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ OP_VAULT (BIP-345)         │ Not activated                            │
  ├────────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ CHECKSIGFROMSTACK          │ Not on Bitcoin mainnet                   │
  └────────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  So "build with covenants that are on mainnet only" is not possible today,
  for anyone. Not just you.
  
  Watch out for this one: crc.garden's material mentions Simplicity.
  Simplicity runs on Liquid — a Blockstream sidechain. It is not Bitcoin. If
  that is where the covenant idea came from, it was misleading.
  
  What you can use on mainnet today

  ┌─────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │        Tool         │                  What it does                   │
  ├─────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Taproot             │ Script paths and MAST. Spending conditions, not │
  │                     │  output restrictions.                           │
  ├─────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ CLTV / CSV          │ Timelocks. Constrain when a coin moves — never  │
  │                     │ where.                                          │
  ├─────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Pre-signed          │ The real-world workaround. You pre-sign the     │
  │ transactions + key  │ only allowed spends, then destroy the key.      │
  │ deletion            │ Users must trust the key was actually           │
  │                     │ destroyed.                                      │
  ├─────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Multisig / MuSig2 / │ A group controls the funds. Federated trust,    │
  │  FROST              │ not a covenant.                                 │
  └─────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  That last group is what every "Bitcoin vault" in production actually does.
  It is trust-minimised, not trustless.
  
  What this means for you

  Your liquidity pool cannot be enforced by Bitcoin. Not with covenants,
  because they do not exist.
  
  Your realistic options are:

  1. Pre-signed + key deletion — closest to a covenant. Publicly verifiable
  ceremony. Users trust the ceremony, not you.
  2. Multisig federation — several independent parties hold the pool. Users
  trust that they do not collude.
  3. Be honest about custody — you hold it. Say so plainly.
  
  All three are honest. None is trustless.

  One caveat

  My knowledge runs to May 2026. A soft fork could have activated since then —
  it is unlikely on that timeline, but I will not guess on something this
  decisive.
  
  Want me to check the current activation status properly? It is a 2-minute
  research job and it settles your whole architecture.

⏺ Decoded. There are no covenants in this transaction. It is not close.

  The proof is in the witness

  Both inputs spend from a Taproot address. Each witness is exactly one 
  64-byte item:

  8a2e1446...042ece5c   ← 64 bytes. A signature. That's all.

  That is a key-path spend. One person, one key, one signature. Nothing else.

  A covenant would look different. You would see a witness with three or more
  items: the arguments, then the script, then a control block. The script is
  where a covenant lives.

  There is no script here. There is nothing to enforce anything.

  Every output is a plain address

  ┌─────┬───────────┬────────┬───────────────────────────┐
  │  #  │   Type    │ Amount │        What it is         │
  ├─────┼───────────┼────────┼───────────────────────────┤
  │ 0   │ OP_RETURN │ 0      │ data                      │
  ├─────┼───────────┼────────┼───────────────────────────┤
  │ 1   │ P2PKH     │ 546    │ Satoshi's genesis address │
  ├─────┼───────────┼────────┼───────────────────────────┤
  │ 2   │ OP_RETURN │ 0      │ data                      │
  ├─────┼───────────┼────────┼───────────────────────────┤
  │ 3   │ P2TR      │ 330    │ plain wallet              │
  ├─────┼───────────┼────────┼───────────────────────────┤
  │ 4   │ P2TR      │ 10,000 │ plain wallet — the fee    │
  ├─────┼───────────┼────────┼───────────────────────────┤
  │ 5   │ P2TR      │ 4,459  │ change                    │
  └─────┴───────────┴────────┴───────────────────────────┘

  No conditions. No locks. No scripts. The 10,000-sat fee goes to an ordinary 
  single-key wallet, same as any personal address.

  Three things you should see

  1. They burn 546 sats to Satoshi's address.

  1A1zP1eP5QGefi2DMPTfTL5SLmv7DivfNa is the genesis block address. Nobody has
  that key. Every transfer throws 546 sats into the void.

  2. Two different protocols in one transaction:

  {"p":"ico-20","op":"transfer","tick":"LEAF","amt":"208231.81860435"}
  {"p":"crc-20","op":"mint","tick":"LEAF"}

  One ico-20 transfer and one crc-20 mint. Two OP_RETURNs, two protocol tags,
  one transaction. That is overloaded and hard to reason about.

  3. The amount has a decimal point.

  "amt":"208231.81860435"

  That is a genuine hazard. How many decimals are allowed? What rounds up,
  what rounds down? What if someone writes 208231.818604350? Two indexers can
  read that differently and both think they are right.

  Your Cove design already fixed this — fixed-width binary integers, no
  decimals. That was the right call.

  So, to your question

  They are not using covenants. Not in the roadmap sense, not in the partial
  sense. This is plain Taproot key-path spends with JSON in OP_RETURN, judged
  by a private server.

  It is architecturally the same thing you built — except yours uses binary
  instead of decimal strings, and your indexer is open.

  Agent 1 is confirming from the BIP files whether covenants exist on mainnet
  at all. Agent 3 is finding where you could actually build if they do not.
  Those two decide your next move.

  🔴 That transaction refutes the "soft covenant state machine" claim

  I decoded it. Here is the whole thing:

  Input: one P2TR, witness = 1 item, 64 bytes. That is a key-path spend — a
  single signature. No script, no control block, nothing to enforce anything.

  Outputs:

  0  OP_RETURN  {"p":"ico-20","op":"transfer","tick":"LEAF","amt":"1630000"}
  1  546 sats → Satoshi's genesis address
  2  OP_RETURN  {"p":"crc-20","op":"mint","tick":"LEAF"}
  3  330 sats → P2TR
  4  10,000 sats → their "leaf" vanity treasury
  5  847,994 sats → ???

  Output 5 is byte-for-byte the same script as the input. I checked:

  INPUT script == vout5 script ?  True

  What that means

  A state machine sends money to a new address that commits to new state. S0 →
  S1.

  This sends money back to the same address it came from. Same key, same
  address, before and after.

  That is not a state machine. That is a wallet spending itself and taking 
  change — exactly like your own wallet does every time you pay for coffee.

  The other assistant told you crc.garden runs Taproot state commitment → 
  policy check → guardian authorizes → mainnet tx.

  The chain does not show that. It shows one key signing, OP_RETURN carrying
  the meaning, and change coming home.

  They were reasoning from the papers. I read the transaction.

  Where the authority actually is

  The OP_RETURN says "op":"mint". Nothing on-chain enforces that mint. No
  script checks supply. No output commits to a successor state.

  Their closed indexer decides what it means. That is the whole security
  model.

  So the "OP_RETURN is just metadata over a real state machine" framing is
  backwards. The OP_RETURN is the ledger. There is no state machine under it.

  What's landing

  packages/cove-market/
    order/  psbt/  quotes/  reconciliation/  service/  store/  testing/

  Six new tables:

  coveV3MarketListings       coveV3MarketListingInputs
  coveV3MarketFills          coveV3MarketCancellations
  coveV3MarketTrades         coveV3MarketEvents

  BIP-322 for listing auth is the right call — the seller proves they control
  the address without spending anything. That's what Magic Eden and every
  serious Ordinals market uses.

  Separating listings from trades from events is also right. Listings are your
  app's opinion; trades are on-chain fact. Keeping them apart means a bad
  listing can never corrupt the ledger.

  Three things to watch as this lands

  1. The listing must commit to specific UTXOs. There's a listingInputs table,
  which suggests they got this. If a listing only says "I'll sell 1M FROG",
  the seller can spend those tokens elsewhere and the fill fails at broadcast.
  Pinning exact outpoints is what makes a listing real.

  2. SIGHASH_SINGLE|ANYONECANPAY is the pattern — it's what crc.garden uses
  and it works. The trap: that sighash lets a buyer add inputs and outputs
  freely. Your validation has to check the final assembled transaction, not
  just the seller's half.

  3. Fee. They charge 7.5% + 5,000 sats. You said 2%. Make it config, not a
  constant — you'll want to change it without a protocol change.

  Still open, and unchanged

  The Guardian is still one key. The market doesn't change that. When someone
  buys, a Guardian signature moves Cove state — and whoever holds that WIF can
  move it anywhere.

  Market first is a defensible call. Just don't take real money until that key
  is split.

  🎉 The Guardian key problem is architecturally closed

  This was my last blocker for six rounds. Look at what landed:

  packages/cove-guardian/src/v3/custody.ts

  interface GuardianCustodyBackend
  interface GuardianSigningBackend
    localSigningBackend(signer)      ← dev
    custodySigningBackend(backend)   ← production
    UnconfiguredGuardianCustodyBackend  ← fails closed

  Plus a standalone HTTP Guardian service with a transport abstraction.

  What that means: the Guardian can now run as its own service, on its own
  machine, signing through a real custody backend. The signing key no longer
  has to live in your app. You plug in an HSM, a hardware signer, or a remote
  custody service behind that interface.

  That's the right shape — better than hardcoding MuSig2, because now you can
  choose.

  Also landed: SIGNED_BUT_AUDIT_FINALIZATION_FAILED. That's the nasty edge
  case where a signature succeeds but the audit log write fails. They handled
  it and keep the journal reserved so the same request can't be double-signed.
  That's careful work.

  ## 1. V1 reorg workflow — fixed (was flaky, now green)                      
                                                                              
  Diagnosis confirmed: the `regtest-reorg.ts` script restarts bitcoind with   
  an empty mempool, but the RPC goes down **before** the datadir `LOCK` + RPC 
  port are released, so the immediate daemon restart flaked with `bitcoind    
  exited with code 1`. Fix: a 2s settle delay + up to 5 retries around the    
  daemon start. **Green** on `e0733fc` (57s) and `68a3913` (37s) — the V1     
  path is not dead, so I kept it and made it reliable rather than deleting    
  it.                                                                         
                                                                              
  ## 2. Offline keygen ceremony tool                                          
                                                                              
  `packages/cove-vault/src/ceremony-keys.ts` + `scripts/ceremony/README.md`,  
  run as `pnpm cove:ceremony-keys --out <dir>`:                               
  - Generates **1 Guardian + 3 recovery** keys via `crypto.randomBytes(32)`.  
  - Prints **only** x-only BIP340 pubkeys (no parity byte).                   
  - Writes each private key to a **separate** `0600` file under a gitignored  
  path — **never** to stdout or the repo; refuses to overwrite existing keys. 
  - Emits a per-key storage checklist.                                        
  - Verified end-to-end (modes `-rw-------`, no private key on stdout), then  
  deleted the test keys.

  The three things I most want answered

  1. Can a buyer rob a seller? SIGHASH_SINGLE|ANYONECANPAY commits the seller
  to one output and lets the buyer add whatever they like. If the final
  assembled transaction isn't re-validated before broadcast, a buyer can take
  tokens and redirect the payment. This is the classic Ordinals-marketplace
  bug and it has cost people real money.

  2. Does an empty allowlist mean nobody, or everybody?
  canary.allowedWalletScripts: [] in the template. If empty reads as "no
  restriction", your caps evaporate the moment the profile is half-filled.
  One-line bug, total bypass.

  3. Is maxBackingSats cumulative or per-operation? If it's per-op, ten
  operations of 200,000 sats blow straight past your 0.01 BTC ceiling. And if
  it is cumulative, is the running total durable and race-safe?

  🔴 The worst one: anyone can permanently brick a token for the price of a tx
  fee

  The Guardian signs at build time — before the user has signed anything:

  cove-app/src/service.ts:432 — transitionSigner.signMint(req) inside
  buildBackingBuy.

  That commits a journal reservation on the backing UTXO. And:

  - The reservation is never released. No delete, no TTL, no expiry. I grepped
  — nothing.
  - The build route has no auth and no rate limit. There is no middleware.ts
  at all.

  The attack:
  1. POST /api/v3/backing/buy/build — Guardian signs, digest committed
  2. Never broadcast. Spend your own funding UTXOs elsewhere 
  3. Backing outpoint unchanged on-chain forever

  Every future request — any buyer, any amount — produces a different digest →
  BACKING_ALREADY_SIGNED. The token is dead permanently. Only the 2-of-3
  offline recovery ceremony gets the BTC back.

  And this fires by accident: every abandoned checkout, every closed browser
  tab, every timed-out wallet prompt bricks that token. On day one that's not
  an if.

  🔴 The two-word bug

  psbt.validateSignaturesOfInput(inputIndex, () => true)

  In both cove-market/src/psbt.ts:57 and cove-app/src/psbt.ts:34.

  That callback is the signature check. It returns true unconditionally. So
  every signature validates — including garbage bytes.

  Every *_SIGNATURE_INVALID error in your codebase is dead code. Your only
  real signature check is testmempoolaccept at the very end.

  Fix: (pubkey, msghash, sig) => ecc.verify(msghash, pubkey, sig)

  🔴 BIP-322 authenticates the wrong key

  order/signature.ts:99-105

  const pubkey = Buffer.from(witness[1]!);   // ← attacker supplies this
  return ecc.verify(Buffer.from(sighash), pubkey, decoded.signature);

  The pubkey comes from the attacker's own witness and is never checked
  against the HASH160 in the address.

  Anyone can forge a listing or a cancellation for any address. The auditor
  proved it:

  ▎ Attacker (key 0x22) forged listing auth for VICTIM (key 0x11) script: 
  ▎ ACCEPTED = true

  So: cancel anyone's listing at will, impersonate any seller, list tokens you
  don't own.

  Fix: require hash160(pubkey) to equal the 20-byte program before verifying.

⏺ Fixed. All green.

  What I fixed

  The bug: guardianXOnly and recovery.pubkeys were only checked with a regex —
  /^[0-9a-f]{64}$/. A hex string that isn't a point on the secp256k1 curve
  passed validation.

  Why that's dangerous: an off-curve key produces a tapleaf no signature can 
  ever satisfy. And because the keys derive the vault address, you only find
  out after you've funded it. Money gone, permanently.

  The agent fixed this for the recovery leaf builder (C8) but missed the
  profile validator — which is where it matters, because that's the gate on
  your committed values.

  The proof it was real

  Their own test fixture contained an off-curve key:

  "11".repeat(32) on-curve:  false

  K1 in profile.test.ts, and the guardianXOnly in three cove-app test files.
  Every one of those would have built an unspendable vault, and the suite was
  green.

  Changes
  
  packages/cove-mainnet/src/profile.ts
  - Added tiny-secp256k1
  - New isXOnlyKey() — regex and ecc.isXOnlyPoint()
  - Applied to guardianXOnly and every recovery.pubkeys entry
  - New check: GUARDIAN_KEY_IN_RECOVERY_SET — the Guardian must not be one of
  the three recovery keys, or your "2-of-3 independent" is really 2-of-2 with
  the Guardian holding one 

  packages/cove-mainnet/src/profile.test.ts — 4 new tests, fixtures moved to
  on-curve keys
  packages/cove-app/src/{mainnet,readiness,readiness-probes}.test.ts —
  off-curve fixtures replaced

  Verified

  typecheck   38 / 38
  lint        37 / 37
  test        37 / 37

  cove-mainnet went 17 → 21 tests. cove-app 45 passing.

  ⚠️  Two things for you

  1. Nothing is committed. 110+ files uncommitted now, including my fix and
  all the agent's security work. Get it committed and pushed.

  2. When you generate your real keys, this now protects you. If
  cove:ceremony-keys ever emits an off-curve value, or you fat-finger a hex
  digit copying it into the profile, readiness --static will reject it before
  you fund anything.

  Still open from the audits: C9 readiness literals, verifyMainnetGenesis
  called from nowhere, M3 client intent verification, M4 rate limiting. None
  of those can brick a vault — they're next, not now.

⏺ No. Generating keys is necessary but not sufficient. Here's exactly what's
  left.

  🔴 The real blocker: there is no production custody backend

  apps/guardian/src/custody.ts now correctly refuses to boot if you use a test
  key on mainnet:

  if (network === "mainnet" && testKeyHex) {
    throw new Error("GUARDIAN_TEST_KEY_HEX is forbidden on mainnet");
  }

  That's the right guard. But it leaves you with exactly two options on
  mainnet:

  ┌──────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Option  │                          Result                           │
  ├──────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Test key │ Refuses to boot ✅                                        │
  ├──────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ No key   │ UnconfiguredGuardianCustodyBackend — throws on everything │
  └──────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  So the mainnet Guardian literally cannot sign anything today. Not a bug —
  the fail-closed design working. But it means generating keys doesn't get you
  to mainnet, because there is nowhere to put the Guardian key that the code
  will accept.

  Somebody has to write a real backend — hardware signer, KMS, or HSM —
  implementing GuardianCustodyBackend. That's the long pole, and it hasn't
  started.

  🔴 Three more open

  ┌──────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                      │                     Status                      │
  ├──────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Rate limiting        │ lib/rate-limit.ts exists, has tests, is called  │
  │                      │ by no route                                     │
  ├──────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │                      │ Now imported by service.ts:41 — but still never │
  │ verifyMainnetGenesis │  invoked. Chain identity unverified on the live │
  │                      │  path                                           │
  ├──────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Client intent (M3)   │ P2P buy/sell still blind-sign the server's PSBT │
  └──────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  🔴 And the one I'd refuse to skip

  You have never tested recovery.

  If the Guardian key is lost or that box dies, the 2-of-3 recovery leaf is
  the only way your BTC comes back. Nobody has ever executed it — not on
  regtest, not on signet.

  I just fixed a bug where an off-curve key would have made the vault
  permanently unspendable. That's the bug class here: recovery failures are 
  invisible until you need recovery.

  Rehearse it on signet, against the exact MAINNET1 profile shape, before real
  BTC goes in.

  Honest answer to your question

  Generating keys is step 1 of about 4.

  ┌─────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────────┬─────────────┐
  │  #  │                                                   │    Time     │
  ├─────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────┤
  │ 1   │ Commit + push everything (110 files uncommitted   │ minutes     │
  │     │ right now)                                        │             │
  ├─────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────┤
  │ 2   │ Generate keys                                     │ 20 min      │
  ├─────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────┤
  │ 3   │ Write a production custody backend                │ the long    │
  │     │                                                   │ pole        │
  ├─────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────┼─────────────┤
  │ 4   │ Rehearse 2-of-3 recovery on signet                │ half a day  │
  └─────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────┴─────────────┘

  Steps 3 and 4 are what stand between you and mainnet. Not the keys.

  If you want the fastest legitimate path

  Pick the simplest custody backend that isn't an env var. A hardware signer
  you already own, wrapped behind GuardianCustodyBackend, is days — not weeks.
  A cloud KMS is a similar order.

  Then rehearse recovery. Then you're ready.

  Right now, today: get those 110 files committed. That's real work sitting
  unprotected, including every security fix from three audits and mine.

⏺ All 10 workflows green. Everything committed and pushed. Here's where you
  stand.

  What I did

  Committed and pushed the 110 uncommitted files — three audits' worth of
  security work that was sitting unprotected. Four commits, all CI-green.

  Then found and fixed three more bugs:

  1. Off-curve keys could brick your vault permanently. guardianXOnly and
  recovery.pubkeys were regex-checked only. An off-curve key makes a tapleaf
  no signature can satisfy — and since the keys derive the vault address,
  you'd only discover it after funding. Their own test fixture contained one
  ("11".repeat(32) is off-curve) and validated clean. Now curve-checked, plus
  a new GUARDIAN_KEY_IN_RECOVERY_SET check so your 2-of-3 isn't secretly
  2-of-2.

  2. Your go/no-go tool exited 0 on NOT_READY. Any automation gating on exit
  code read a failed readiness check as success.

  3. 🔴 The signing journal broke under concurrency. This is the important
  one. CI caught it:

  ▎ 20-concurrent race → expected 1 RESERVED, got 6

  reserve() did SELECT → unconditional DELETE → INSERT. Twenty concurrent
  callers each saw "absent", each deleted the row a peer had just committed,
  each inserted. Six callers would each believe they held the same backing 
  UTXO — the double-sign guard failing exactly under load. Replaced with a
  single atomic upsert. Race now yields exactly 1.

  Also wired rate limiting to all 31 routes (16 were unprotected) with a
  coverage test that fails the build if anyone adds an unprotected route — it
  immediately caught a GET handler the sweep missed.

  And rebuilt the readiness CI to run a real Guardian against real Postgres,
  asserting three negative cases: no Guardian → NOT_READY, unauthenticated →
  401, wrong committed hash → NOT_READY.

  ---
  Where you are for launch

  Ready: the protocol, the settlement, the policy engine, the Taproot maths,
  the curve. Three adversarial audits found no path to stealing funds.

  🔴 Two blockers remain, both yours:

  1. No production custody backend. The Guardian correctly refuses to boot on
  mainnet with a test key, and the only alternative throws on everything. So
  the mainnet Guardian cannot sign at all today. Someone must implement
  GuardianCustodyBackend against real hardware or a KMS. This hasn't started.

  2. Readiness needs more than I'd said. The probes are real now —
  indexerHealthy, stateRootVerified, workerHealthy, releaseManifestOk require
  a synced indexer, a held worker lock, and committed state-root and
  release-manifest hashes. That's live infrastructure, not just a config file.

  And one thing I'd refuse to skip: you have still never executed a 2-of-3
  recovery. I just fixed a bug where a bad key would have made recovery
  impossible — undetectably, after funding. Rehearse it on signet before real 
  BTC goes in.

  Honest estimate: custody backend is days. Recovery rehearsal is half a day.
  Then you're ready.

⏺ Good catch — and the answer is: both, deliberately.

  packages/cove-wire/src/opcodes.ts:13
  export const COVE_PROTOCOL_ID = "cove-20";

  Your wire tag is cove-20, not crc-20. That's the right call and it was
  deliberate — if you used crc-20, your tokens would land in crc.garden's
  ledger and their closed indexer would decide what your tokens mean. cove-20
  keeps your protocol yours.

  So the accurate framing, which matches what you told me earlier — CRC 
  publicly, honest in the technical docs:

  - Category / narrative: CRC. That's the space you're in and what you tell
  people.
  - Implementation: Cove, wire tag cove-20, your own indexer, your own rules.

  What you'd gain

  Using crc-20 as your tag would mean:

  - Their market could trade them

  That's genuinely valuable. It's why the question is worth asking.

  The decisive problem

  The tag isn't a label. It's an address to a ledger.

  If you emit {"p":"crc-20","op":"deploy","tick":"FROG"}, then their closed 
  indexer decides whether FROG exists, what its supply is, and who owns what.

  You'd be building a product whose entire state is determined by software you
  cannot read, run, or check.

  That is the exact thing you rejected when you built Cove.

  Four more, concrete

  1. You'd need their permission, and they never gave it.
  Question 1 of the 30 you wrote: "Can third-party applications request 
  arbitrary CRC-20 deployment?" Never answered. And their public contract
  requires an oracle signature for DEPLOY and MINT — meaning they'd have to
  sign every launch.

  2. Nobody has ever deployed a second one.
  Their activity page: Deploys: 1. Only LEAF, months in. It's unproven that a
  second CRC-20 token can exist at all.

  3. Your fees would go to them.
  Their mint pays 10,000 sats to bc1phuuulh7...spyleaf — their treasury. Adopt
  their format and your launchpad's revenue lands in their wallet unless they
  agree otherwise. Which is, again, question 1.

  4. Their format is technically worse than yours.

  theirs:
  {"p":"ico-20","op":"transfer","tick":"LEAF","amt":"208231.81860435"}
  yours:   COVE | ver | op | tick | u64 amount   (26 bytes, fixed-width)

  That decimal is a real hazard. How many decimal places are legal? Does
  208231.818604350 equal it? Two indexers can read it differently and both
  think they're right. Their users are already posting "why my $leaf balance 
  0?"

  Your binary format makes that class of bug structurally impossible — which
  is why 16 parser tests got deleted as obsolete when you switched.

  What you keep for free

  The narrative costs nothing and needs nobody's permission. You can say
  "CRC", sit in the category, use the vocabulary, reference the same timeline.

  What you don't hand over is the ledger.

  The honest summary

  If they ever answer question 1 and open their indexer, revisiting this
  becomes sensible — and your CanonicalCRCProvider seam means it wouldn't be a
  rewrite.

  Until then, adopting their tag means asking permission to run your own
  product, from people who haven't replied in months.

⏺ I was wrong about the main risk. Let me correct that.

  My objection doesn't hold for your architecture

  I said "shared tag = shared ledger = their indexer decides your state."

  BONS just disproved it. They use p:"crc-20" and crc.garden returns not_found
  for them. Nobody joined anyone's ledger. crc-20 is behaving as an open 
  namespace with independent indexers.

  And your architecture was already immune to the collision problem I raised:

  codecV2.ts:13 — "Post-deploy messages carry the 32-byte tokenId explicitly."

  Your identity is the deploy txid, not the ticker. Two FROGs from different
  deploys are different tokens. The ambiguity I warned about doesn't exist
  here.

  So: your call is sound. Doing it.

  The cost is almost nothing

  COVE_PROTOCOL_ID appears in exactly one place — an export. Your wire format
  is binary with a 2-byte magic; the string isn't in the bytes. Changing the
  label is a one-line change.

  But here's the real decision

  A label change is invisible. Nobody discovers you from a constant in your 
  source.

  crc.garden's own transactions carry two envelopes — ico-20 and crc-20 — in
  one transaction. That's how their tokens are readable by different parsers.

  So you have a fork:

  A — Label only. You call it CRC-20 in docs and marketing. Your wire stays
  pure binary. Cheap, zero risk, zero discoverability. Nobody's explorer sees
  your tokens.

  B — Dual envelope. Keep your binary envelope as the authority, and emit a
  small crc-20 JSON envelope alongside it for discovery. Your tokens become
  visible to any crc-20 indexer or explorer. This is exactly what crc.garden
  does.

  B is what actually gets you their audience. A costs nothing and buys
  nothing.

  The cost of B: one extra OP_RETURN output per transaction (~30-60 sats of
  dust and fee), a spec decision about what goes in the JSON, and a clear rule
  that the binary envelope is authoritative and the JSON is advisory — so a
  lying JSON can never change your state.

  My recommendation

  Do B, with the authority rule written into the validator. You get the
  namespace, the discoverability, and the audience — while your state still
  comes from bytes that can't be misread.

  Want me to implement it? I'd:
  1. Flip COVE_PROTOCOL_ID to "crc-20"
  2. Add the JSON discovery envelope to the builder
  3. Make the validator ignore it for state and reject any transaction where
  it contradicts the binary envelope
  4. Tests proving a hostile JSON envelope changes nothing

  Say go and I'll do it.

⏺ Done. 11 workflows green, including the new relay proof.
  
  What shipped

  You are crc-20 now.

  export const COVE_PROTOCOL_ID = "crc-20";

  And your transactions can carry a second OP_RETURN that any CRC indexer can
  read:

  vout0  6a...43560203aaaa…              ← binary envelope (AUTHORITY)
  vout1  witness_v0_keyhash              ← payment
  vout2  {"p":"crc-20","op":"mint","tick":"FROG","amt":"1000000"}   ←
  discovery

  Broadcast and mined on real Bitcoin Core. That's crc.garden's exact layout.

  The authority rule is enforced, not documented

  The indexer reads vout 0 and nothing else (parser.ts:35). The discovery
  envelope never touches state.

  And discoveryAgreesWithBinary() re-derives the canonical payload from the
  binary message and demands byte equality. A lying JSON can't even be
  published under a Cove signature. Tests prove rejection of:

  - wrong amount · wrong ticker · wrong operation
  - reordered keys · injected whitespace · extra fields · junk

  Two things I found by measuring instead of assuming

  1. The relay boundary is real.

  Core 28.1  →  allowed=false   "multi-op-return"
  Core 31.1  →  allowed=true    broadcast + mined

  Core 30 relaxed the datacarrier policy. Your CI runs 28.1, which is why the
  new proof pins 31.1 — and I confirmed the test genuinely fails on 28.1 with
  a clear diagnostic rather than passing vacuously.

  This means: emitting the envelope needs a Core ≥30 relay path. Most of
  mainnet is there now (that's how crc.garden's tx confirmed), but nodes on
  ≤29 won't relay it.

  over the 80-byte limit. So it's ticker-keyed, exactly like every crc-20
  envelope in the wild. Your binary envelope still carries the real tokenId,

  The wire layer is done and proven. The builder doesn't emit it yet — I
  deliberately stopped there, because wiring it into builder.ts shifts output
  indices and the validator caps output counts at fixed positions. That's a
  change I want to make carefully with the Guardian's output validation, not
  bolt on at the end of a long session.

  Next step is: add an opt-in discoveryEnvelope flag to the mainnet profile,
  append the output last, bump the validator's output cap by one when present,
  and reject any transaction where the JSON contradicts the binary.

⏺ Done. All 11 workflows green.
  
  You are crc-20 now, end to end

  export const COVE_PROTOCOL_ID = "crc-20";

  And a Cove mint can carry a readable envelope any CRC indexer parses:

  vout0  6a...43560203aaaa…                                      ← binary
  (AUTHORITY)
  vout1  vault  ·  vout2  carrier  ·  vout3  fee  ·  vout4  change
  vout5  {"p":"crc-20","op":"mint","tick":"FROG","amt":"8400000000000000"}

  The authority rule is enforced by code, not by comment

  Three independent barriers:

  1. The indexer reads vout 0 and nothing else (parser.ts:35). The JSON is
  structurally incapable of reaching state.
  2. The Guardian refuses to sign a transaction whose JSON contradicts the
  binary envelope → DISCOVERY_MISMATCH. So a misleading payload can't be
  published under your signature at all.
  3. The envelope is appended last. A test asserts vout 0..n-1 are
  byte-identical with and without it — no index shifted, no existing check
  weakened.

  Rejection is proven for: wrong amount, wrong ticker, wrong op, reordered
  keys, whitespace, extra fields, an envelope carrying sats, and a ticker when
  the caller declared none.

  The constraint you need to know

  I measured this rather than trusting a changelog:

  ┌───────────┬─────────────────────────────────┐
  │           │                                 │
  ├───────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Core 28.1 │ allowed=false — multi-op-return │
  ├───────────┼─────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Core 31.1 │ broadcast and mined ✅          │
  └───────────┴─────────────────────────────────┘

  Core 30 relaxed the datacarrier policy. So this is opt-in —
  discoveryEnvelope defaults off. Turn it on and your transactions need a Core
  ≥30 relay path. Most of mainnet is there (that's how crc.garden's tx
  confirms), but older nodes won't forward it.

  A dedicated CI job pins Core 31.1 and proves the relay on every push — and I
  confirmed the test genuinely fails on 28.1 rather than passing vacuously.

  Also worth knowing

  No tokenId fits. 64 hex chars pushes the payload to 128 bytes, over the
  80-byte limit — so it's ticker-keyed, exactly like every crc-20 envelope in
  the wild. Your binary envelope still carries the real 32-byte tokenId, so
  identity stays exact where it matters.

  Verified
  
  typecheck 37/37 · lint 37/37 · test 37/37 · build 21/21
  cove-wire      45 → 59 tests
  cove-guardian 108 → 122 tests
  11/11 CI workflows green

  What's left

  The envelope is off by default. To use it: pass discoveryEnvelope: { ticker 
  } in the builder and discoveryTicker to the validator. Wiring that through
  the app service and the mainnet profile is the last step — say the word.

⏺ Done — both parts.

  1. The crc-20 envelope is finished

  COVE_V3_DISCOVERY_ENVELOPE now runs config → service → builder → Guardian.
  Default off. Turn it on and your mints carry a readable {"p":"crc-20",...}
  output any CRC indexer can parse, while the binary envelope at vout 0 stays
  the only thing that touches state.

  2. New design — the "Ledger" system
  
  Go look: http://localhost:3000 — it's running.

  What changed:
  - Monospace throughout, zero rounding, 1px hairlines. Bone panels on ink,
  faint engineering grid behind it.
  - One accent — signal amber. Green/amber/red are now reserved for protocol 
  state only, never decoration. A colour on screen means something. 
  - Tabular figures + slashed zero globally. Every number here is meant to be
  read precisely.

  The homepage leads with your actual claim rather than a slogan, puts the
  frozen constants (840M / 160M / 0.242 BTC / 20 stages) where a visitor sees
  them first, and states the trust boundary as a two-column table:

  ▎ Consensus — Bitcoin enforces the signature, the UTXO rules, the successor 
  ▎ output
  ▎ Policy — the Guardian enforces supply and the curve. Bitcoin will not 
  ▎ reject an invalid Cove transition.

  That honesty is the one thing crc.garden and BONS can't say. It belongs on
  the front page, not buried in docs.

  Verified: typecheck 37/37, lint 37/37, test 37/37, build 21/21. Pushed.

  ---
  How to test the rest

  pnpm cove:liquidity-demo          # full lifecycle, instant, no deps
  pnpm dev:web                      # the UI you're looking at

  And I installed Bitcoin Core while testing the relay, so these work now too:

  pnpm cove:regtest-proof           # state-committed vault spend
  pnpm cove:v3-regtest-lifecycle    # DEPLOY → MINT → TRANSFER → REDEEM
  pnpm cove:regtest-reorg           # reorg → recovered root == clean replay

  Two notes

  One page still needs work. I restyled the homepage, header and token cards
  by hand; the other five pages picked up the palette through the class
  migration but haven't been composed in the new system — they'll look
  consistent but not designed. Say which matters most and I'll do it properly.

  A warning worth keeping: I found earlier that a naive regex broke every .tsx
  file. I reverted and redid it scoped to className strings only.
  Everything's verified green — but that's why the build cache needed clearing
  mid-way.

⏺ Fixed. Refresh your browser — it should look like this now.

  What happened

  Not a code problem. I ran pnpm build (production) while pnpm dev was
  running. They share apps/web/.next, so the production build overwrote the
  dev server's chunks. Every JS and CSS asset started 500'ing with
  MODULE_NOT_FOUND, and the browser rendered raw unstyled HTML.

  Cleared .next, restarted dev. CSS now serves 200.

  My mistake — I should have stopped the dev server before running the full
  build.

  Avoiding it

  Don't run these at the same time. If the page ever goes unstyled again,
  that's the signature:

  pkill -f "next dev" && rm -rf apps/web/.next && pnpm dev:web

  Where things stand

  http://localhost:3000

  Homepage, launch, header and token cards are composed in the Ledger system.
  The other four pages — explore, market, activity, wallet — picked up the
  palette but haven't been laid out properly yet. They'll look consistent, not
  designed.

  Everything is committed and pushed. Which page do you want next?

  What you're seeing

  Aggregate row first — 6 tokens, 0.864 BTC total backing, 5,960 holders. The
  shape of the whole set before any single token.

  Six fixture tokens spanning the states that actually differ visually:

  ┌────────┬─────────────┬────────────────────────┐
  │        │  Progress   │         State          │
  ├────────┼─────────────┼────────────────────────┤
  │ REEF   │ 840M / 840M │ At cap                 │
  ├────────┼─────────────┼────────────────────────┤
  │ HARBOR │ 834.9M      │ 99.4%, nearly there    │         
  ├────────┼─────────────┼────────────────────────┤
  │ ANCHOR │ 657.7M      │ mid-late, stage 16     │
  ├────────┼─────────────┼────────────────────────┤
  │ TIDE   │ 432.6M      │ halfway, no ask listed │
  ├────────┼─────────────┼────────────────────────┤
  │ SATCAT │ 199.9M      │ early                  │
  ├────────┼─────────────┼────────────────────────┤
  │ FROG   │ 35.2M       │ fresh launch, stage 1  │
  └────────┴─────────────┴────────────────────────┘

  Two views. Grid for browsing, table for scanning — hairline rules, tabular
  numerals, inline progress bars. Once you have more than a dozen tokens the
  table is the one people will live in.

  Filters and sorts: all / open / at cap / listed · progress / backing /
  holders / newest.

  Three distinct empty states, not one generic message:
  - No tokens at all → offers Launch the first one
  - No search match → offers Clear search
  - Indexer unreachable → rejected chip, and says explicitly the page is
  read-only so nobody thinks their wallet broke

  Loading renders a skeleton in the result's shape, so the layout doesn't jump
  when data lands.

  A real bug fell out of this

  Your amounts were rendering as 8400000B.

  fmtTokens takes atoms but never divided by 1e8. So 840,000,000 tokens
  displayed as "84000000B" — on every page that showed a token amount. Cards,
  tables, token detail, wallet.

  Fixed, with 7 tests pinning the cap, the reserve, decimal handling and
  sub-token truncation. Web tests went 37 → 44.

  How demo mode works

  ?demo=1 is a client-side render path only. It never calls the API, never
  writes, is inert without the query param, and labels itself on screen as
  "Demo data · not from the chain." So you can review any page populated
  without seeding a database.

  I'll add it to the other pages as I redesign them.

  The faucet

  You do not need it. Your signer already holds 487,546 sats on Mutinynet.
  That is enough to run the proof now.

  (If you ever do need more, you must paste the address at the faucet
  yourself. It has a captcha. I will not go around it.)

  The charts

  Real candlestick charts, one per token. KLineCharts, Apache-2.0, free to
  use.

  - Painted in your Ledger colours. Not the library's default rainbow.
  - Green candle = price up. Red = price down. Same meaning as the rest of the
  app.
  - 4 time buttons: 10M, 1H, 4H, 1D.
  - Ask ladder on the right, with depth bars.
  - Stat strip on top: last, change, high, low, trades.

  The data is real, not fake. I built a new endpoint that reads settled
  peer-to-peer trades from your database. If a block gets reorganised, those
  trades are dropped. A token with no trades shows a message, not a made-up
  line.

  Under ?demo=1 you see a fake series so you can review the design today. It
  is labelled DEMO SERIES on screen.

  Look at it here:
  http://localhost:3000/token/3anchor03anchor03anchor03anchor03anchor03anchor0
  3anchor03anchor0?demo=1

  Checks

  - Build: green, 21/21
  - Tests: 58 pass, 14 of them new for the price math
  - Pushed: commit a2452e4

  One small thing I found but did not fix: when the database is not set up,
  every API returns "Your wallet is connected to the wrong network." That
  message is wrong and will confuse people. It is old, not from today's work.

  What now

  Option A — run the Mutinynet proof. You have the sats. This tests the real
  thing end to end on a test chain. I would pick this. It moves you toward
  mainnet.

  Option B — keep polishing the UI. Add charts to the Explore and Market pages
  too.

  I would go with A.

  What I did

  Explore — grid view gone. Table only, like you asked. The cards showed less
  per row than the table did.

  Every list page now has a price and a trend line. Explore, Market, and the
  home page. The little line charts are drawn as plain SVG, not real charts,
  Market page was still on the old ugly styles. I rebuilt it:

  - It showed a chopped-up token ID. Now it shows the ticker (ANCHOR, FROG). I
  had to join the name into the database query to do this.
  - Ask prices now use sats/1M — the same unit as the charts. You can compare
  an ask to the last trade by eye.
  - Asks are grouped per token, cheapest first inside each group. Before it
  mixed all tokens together by price, which made a cheap token look like a
  bargain against an expensive one. That was wrong.
  - An ask below the last trade shows green.
  - Status uses the colour chips (ACTIVE / RESERVED / BROADCAST).

  Checks

  - Build: green, 21/21
  - Tests: 58 pass
  - Pushed: commit 45d078b

  Look here:
  http://localhost:3000/explore?demo=1
  http://localhost:3000/market?demo=1

  One note: I could not test the new database join for real, because there is
  no database running here. It compiles and the types are right, but it has
  not touched a live database yet.

  What now

  Option A — run the Mutinynet proof. You have 487,546 sats ready. This is the
  step toward mainnet, and it would also test that database join for real.

  Option B — keep polishing. The Activity and Wallet pages are the last two I
  have not touched.

  I would go with A. It covers the untested join too.

⏺ Confirmed. Now I have the full picture. Reporting while the proof scans.
  
  What I found — this matters more than the proof itself.

  Your proof tests the wrong code

  The old Mutinynet proof is real. I checked all three transactions on the
  chain. They are confirmed in blocks 3449406, 3449407, 3449408. I decoded
  them and they hold genuine Cove data.

  But they use the old format, magic word COVE.

  Your website uses a different, newer format, magic word CV, protocol crc-20.

  They are two separate stacks. I verified this four ways:
  - apps/web does not even list the old package as a dependency
  - your CI blocks the app from importing it
  (scripts/check-v3-architecture.mjs:33)
  - every launch/mint/transfer route traces to encodeDeployV2 and friends
  (packages/cove-guardian/src/v3/builder.ts:71)
  - the old indexer says so itself at the top of the file: "LEGACY / 
  REFERENCE... NOT the production token protocol"
  (packages/cove-indexer/src/index.ts:1-7)

  The gap

  ┌────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │         Format         │               Where it has run               │
  ├────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ CV / crc-20 — what     │ regtest only (a fake chain on your own       │
  │ ships                  │ machine)                                     │
  ├────────────────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ COVE — legacy          │ signet, Mutinynet, and a mainnet canary      │
  └────────────────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Your real code has never been relayed by a public Bitcoin network. Only by a
  private one you control. Real networks have real nodes with real relay
  rules that can reject things regtest accepts.

  Also: your live code refuses to broadcast to mainnet on purpose
  (packages/cove-guardian/src/v3/broadcast.ts:23-25). That safety gate is
  still on.

  What I did

  - Verified the old proof is genuine (not just three random transactions)
  - Found and fixed a real bug: changing the ticker kept the old ticker's
  transaction IDs, so the tool jammed on BLOCKED_UNRESOLVED with no way out
  except editing the file by hand. Pushed as dd768d6.
  - Started a fresh proof with ticker KELP. Key control verified, 486,958 sats
  found. It is scanning ~5,000 blocks now, so it will take a few more
  minutes.

  What now

  Option A — build a Mutinynet proof for the real CV format. This is the
  missing piece. It puts your actual shipping code on a public Bitcoin network
  for the first time. The existing script is a good template; it needs the V2
  builders swapped in.

  Option B — let the KELP run finish and stop there. It confirms the pipeline
  works, but only for legacy code.

  I would go with A. B tests code you do not ship.

  The Guardian ran untouched. Its own log shows the Simplicity checker and the
  backup policy checker both said PASS, and the two commitment hashes
  matched. Same path your website uses.

  The Guardian caught a real mistake. My first mint was too small. The 1% fee
  came to 5 sats, below Bitcoin's 294-sat dust floor. The Guardian refused to
  sign and said why: PROTOCOL_FEE_DUST. That is the safety net working, on a
  real network, not in a test.

  Mainnet is still locked. Two separate gates. The script checks the chain's
  birth certificate and refuses mainnet. The broadcast helper refuses mainnet
  outright. Neither was touched.

  - Tests: 37/37

  I would go with B first. It is one more test run and it closes the scariest

  What I tested

  Your vault has an emergency exit: if the Guardian disappears, 2 of your 3
  recovery keys can move the money — but only after a waiting period. It had
  never been run once. Now it has.

  Test 1 — the 2-of-3 lock

  ┌────────────────────────────┬────────────┐
  │        What I tried        │   Result   │
  ├────────────────────────────┼────────────┤
  │ 1 key out of 3             │ Refused ✓  │
  ├────────────────────────────┼────────────┤
  │ 2 keys, too early          │ Refused ✓  │
  ├────────────────────────────┼────────────┤
  │ 2 keys, after the wait     │ Accepted ✓ │
  ├────────────────────────────┼────────────┤
  │ 2 keys, one byte corrupted │ Refused ✓  │
  └────────────────────────────┴────────────┘

  Test 2 — the waiting period (144 blocks)

  ┌───────────────────┬───────────────────────────────┐
  │   What I tried    │            Result             │
  ├───────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┤
  │ Spend immediately │ Refused — "non-BIP68-final" ✓ │
  ├───────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┤
  │ Wait 143 blocks   │ Refused — one block short ✓   │
  ├───────────────────┼───────────────────────────────┤
  │ Wait 144 blocks   │ Accepted, and mined ✓         │
  └───────────────────┴───────────────────────────────┘

  That off-by-one test is the important one. The lock is exact, not
  approximate.

  Bitcoin itself refused these, not our code. I asked a real Bitcoin node each
  time. It said no. That is the only answer that counts.

  A bug I found on the way

  Both recovery scripts talked to Bitcoin the wrong way — they only worked if
  nothing else was running on the node. So the moment your app was running,
  your emergency recovery tool would not start. Exactly when you would need
  it. Fixed.
