⏺ Both answered.
  
  1. What the recovery keys are for

  Normal days, one key does everything: the Guardian key. It signs every buy
  and sell.

  That is also the danger. One key. If it is lost, stolen, or the operator
  walks away, every vault is frozen forever. The BTC sits there and nobody can
  move it.

  The recovery keys are the way out.

  How it works:
  - You make 3 recovery keys.
  - Any 2 of them together can move BTC out of a vault.
  - But only after 144 blocks — about 24 hours.

  Why the 24-hour wait? So a theft is visible before it finishes. If someone
  steals 2 keys and starts a grab, it shows up on the Bitcoin chain and you
  get a day to react. Without the delay, it would be instant and silent.

  That is the exact thing I tested and it passed. Bitcoin itself refused the
  early spend, refused at 143 blocks, and allowed it at 144.

  One rule your code already enforces: the Guardian key is not allowed to be
  one of the 3 recovery keys. The code rejects it
  (GUARDIAN_KEY_IN_RECOVERY_SET). Good — otherwise one break-in takes
  everything.

  So keep the 3 keys in 3 separate places. Three different people, or three
  different safes. If all 3 sit in one folder, the 2-of-3 protection is
  decoration.

  2. Same tech as crc.garden and BONS?

  Yes — same family. Genuinely, not just the name.

  I found the proof inside your own code:

  packages/cove-vault/src/leaves.ts:20
    RECOVERY leaf — mirrors PRECOP yellowpaper §4.3 verbatim

  PRECOP is crc.garden's own spec. Their site calls CRC-20 a "covenant token 
  protocol on Bitcoin L1" using a "client validated" PRECOP model. Your vault
  implements their §4.3 word for word.

  BONS ($BONS) also brands itself CRC-20 on Bitcoin.

  Where you are the same:

  ┌───────────┬──────────────────┬──────────────────┬─────────────────────┐
  │           │       You        │    crc.garden    │        BONS         │
  ├───────────┼──────────────────┼──────────────────┼─────────────────────┤
  │ Namespace │ crc-20           │ crc-20           │ crc-20              │
  ├───────────┼──────────────────┼──────────────────┼─────────────────────┤
  │ Chain     │ Bitcoin L1       │ Bitcoin L1       │ Bitcoin L1          │
  ├───────────┼──────────────────┼──────────────────┼─────────────────────┤
  │ Model     │ client-validated │ client-validated │ client-prepared txs │
  ├───────────┼──────────────────┼──────────────────┼─────────────────────┤
  │ Spec      │ PRECOP           │ PRECOP           │ —                   │
  └───────────┴──────────────────┴──────────────────┴─────────────────────┘

  Where you are different — and this is your actual product:

  You have a backing reserve. Real BTC sits in a Taproot vault. Buy tokens,
  BTC goes in. Sell them back, BTC comes out, at a price fixed by a 20-stage
  curve. I watched it move today: 10,000 → 59,350 sats.

  Neither of the others does that. BONS does buybacks and pays BTC to top
  holders — a different idea entirely.

  You also write your data as compact binary (CV, ~42 bytes). They write JSON.
  Yours is cheaper per transaction.

  The catch you should know

  Calling yourself crc-20 does not put you in crc.garden's indexer. It is an
  open name, not a club with a door. Earlier today I checked their indexer for
  BONS and it came back not found — and BONS is crc-20.

  So being crc-20 gets you the audience and the vocabulary. It does not get
  you their listings for free. If you want to appear there, that is a
  conversation with them, not a code change.

  Want me to dig further?

  Option A — read the PRECOP yellowpaper properly and tell you exactly where
  you match it and where you diverge. Useful before you tell anyone you are
  PRECOP-compatible, because right now that claim rests on one code comment.

  Option B — leave it and go to the ceremony.

  I would do A — it is quick, and you are about to make public claims about
  compatibility. Better to know precisely what is true.

⏺ Traced it. Here's what actually happens today.

  The lifecycle, start to finish:

  1. Launch → a Taproot vault is created with 10,000 sats in it.
  2. People mint → their BTC goes into the vault, tokens come out. Price
  climbs through 20 fixed stages: 500 sats per million → 149,731 per million.
  3. They can sell on the marketplace immediately. No waiting, no gate. I
  checked — the market has no cap check at all. List and trade from block one.
  4. They can also sell back to the vault anytime, at the exact reverse price
  minus fee.
  5. At 840M minted → minting stops. Vault stays. Trading and selling-back
  keep working forever.

  So there is no graduation, and that's deliberate. The liquidity.ts file says
  so in its own header:

  ▎ "DETERMINISTIC SIMULATOR for mock/regtest/testing ONLY... NOT activated on
  ▎ mainnet. The 160M graduation reserve is not a trustless on-chain pool — 
  ▎ it is a virtual pool."

  Nothing in your live code imports it.

  Why it was built this way: pump.fun needs graduation because its curve is
  temporary training wheels until Raydium. Yours never stops. The vault is the
  market, permanently. That's your actual edge — a holder can always cash out
  at a known price, forever.

  But you're right that you're missing the moment. There's no "this token made
  it" event. No reason to watch. That's a real product gap, not a technical
  one.

  That 160M reserve (16% of supply) is sitting unspent, which is exactly what
  you'd fund a graduation with.

  Which way do you want it?

  How they split
  
  One token UTXO goes in, up to 4 token outputs come out (builder.ts:260). So
  you send 30,000 to a buyer and the leftover — 99,630.95238095 — comes back
  to you as change, as a fresh UTXO.
  
  That's what you're seeing in that screenshot. Those odd numbers are change
  from partial sells, not someone deliberately picking a weird amount.
  
  Can people sell 1, or 105, or 99630.952?
  
  Depends where they sell it.
  
  ┌────────────────────────────────┬───────────────┬──────────────┐
  │             Where              │ Smallest bit  │ 99,630.952…? │
  ├────────────────────────────────┼───────────────┼──────────────┤
  │ P2P market (sell to a person)  │ 0.00000001    │ ✅ yes       │
  ├────────────────────────────────┼───────────────┼──────────────┤
  │ Transfer (send to someone)     │ 0.00000001    │ ✅ yes       │
  ├────────────────────────────────┼───────────────┼──────────────┤
  │ Curve (sell back to the vault) │ 1 whole token │ ❌ no        │
  └────────────────────────────────┴───────────────┴──────────────┘
  
  So 1 token ✅, 105 tokens ✅, 99630.95238095 ✅ — on the marketplace.
  
  But the vault refuses fractions. Your code throws SUBTOKEN_REDEEM: amount 
  must be whole token (transitionV2.ts:94). Same on the buy side —
  SUBTOKEN_MINT.
  
  Two things you should decide

  1. A real bug — silent truncation. If someone types 99630.952380952 (9
  decimals), your code quietly chops it to 99630.95238095 and eats the rest
  (format.ts:11, .slice(0, 8)). No warning. They just lose a sliver. Small
  money, but it's silent, and silent is the bad part.
  
  2. The whole-token wall. If someone holds 99,630.95238095 tokens, they can
  sell 99,630 back to the vault but the .95238095 is stuck there forever —
  only sellable to another person. On a launchpad where everyone ends up with
  change from partial fills, most people will have a dusty tail they can't 
  cash out.
  
  That's the real gap versus the screenshot you sent.
  
  Two ways to go:
  
  Option A — let the curve take fractions. Remove the whole-token rule for
  redeem. Honest and complete, everyone can always cash out fully. But it
  touches the covenant state rules the Guardian enforces, so it needs new
  proofs re-run.
  
  Option B — round down in the UI. Keep the rule, but when someone hits "sell
  max", offer 99,630 and say plainly "the remaining 0.95238095 can only be
  sold on the market." Cheap, safe, ships today, but the dust problem stays
  real.
  
  I'd fix the truncation bug either way — that one isn't a choice.
  
  Want A or B? And should I fix the truncation now?

⏺ Decoded it fully. This is the most useful thing you've sent me.
  
  What this transaction actually is
  
  Two sell orders filled at once by one buyer.
  
  IN   670 sats  taproot  ← seller's token         SIGHASH_SINGLE|ANYONECANPAY
  IN   670 sats  taproot  ← seller's token         SIGHASH_SINGLE|ANYONECANPAY
  IN  1000 sats  p2wpkh                            SIGHASH_ALL
  IN 200000 sats taproot  ← buyer's BTC            SIGHASH_DEFAULT
  
  OUT 149840 → seller gets paid
  OUT      0 → OP_RETURN
  {"p":"crc-20","op":"transfer","tick":"LEAF","amt":"3000000000000"}
  OUT   1000 → buyer's token carrier
  OUT  11138 → platform fee
  OUT   1000 → carrier
  OUT  37022 → buyer's change
  
  3000000000000 at 8 decimals = 30,000 LEAF. Miner fee 2,340 sats.
  
  The important bit: SINGLE|ANYONECANPAY
  
  That's the whole trick, and it answers your screenshot.
  
  A seller signs only their own input and their own payout. They don't sign
  the rest of the transaction — they don't know or care who buys it. That
  signed fragment then just sits on the order book.
  
  A buyer comes along, grabs as many of those fragments as they want, staples
  their own BTC to it, and signs once. One transaction, many sellers filled.
  
  That's why your screenshot shows a stack of asks with a "Confirm purchase"
  button. You're sweeping several pre-signed offers in one go.
  
  Now the bad news
  
  Your code deliberately refuses to do this
  (packages/cove-market/src/psbt.ts:49):
  
  ▎ "Rejects ANYONECANPAY" → throws UNSAFE_SIGHASH
  
  You require SIGHASH_ALL from both sides, which forces the reservation dance:
  reserve → build → buyer signs → seller signs → settle. That's why your
  market has RESERVED and BUYER_SIGNED states and theirs doesn't.
  
  Whoever wrote that wasn't wrong — SINGLE|ANYONECANPAY has real footguns —
  but it costs you the order book. You can't sweep. You can't have
  free-floating offers. Every trade needs the seller online-ish.
  
  And the splitting answer
  
  They put the amount in the OP_RETURN and let the leftover stay implicitly
  with the sender. No explicit change allocation. That's why 99,630.95238095
  is nothing special for them — it's just a number in a JSON string.
  
  You allocate explicitly per-UTXO, which is stronger (your state is committed
  on-chain, theirs lives in an indexer) but makes fractions more work.
  
  Two more facts, confirmed from the bytes
  
  - No covenant. Every input is a plain key-path signature. One witness item,
  64 or 65 bytes. No tapscript, no control block. Their "covenant protocol" is
  the same soft model as yours.
  - Their data is 66 bytes of JSON. Yours is ~42 bytes of binary. Yours is
  cheaper per transaction.
  
  ---
  The two agents are still verifying. When they report I'll give you the plan,
  and the sighash decision above will be the biggest item in it — it's the
  difference between a marketplace and an order book.

⏺ Fact-checked every point. Here's your scorecard.
  
  ✅ 1. "Fixed token supply" — RIGHT

  And it's stronger than you think: the creator can't choose it. Every token
  is identical. The DEPLOY transaction carries only a ticker, a nonce, and a
  policy version — no supply field at all. It's hardcoded: "Immutable; never 
  user configurable."

  ❌ 2. "We keep 20%" — WRONG, twice
  
  It's 16% on paper (160M of 1,000,000,000).

  And in reality it's 0%. That 160M is never minted, has no field in your
  on-chain state, and appears in no transaction. You keep no tokens at all.

  What you actually keep is fees:
  - 1% on every curve buy — charged on top of the price
  - 1% on every sell — deducted from the payout
  - 0.5% on peer-to-peer trades 
  - Plus 10,000 sats locked into each vault at launch, which nobody ever gets
  back

  So your revenue is a toll, not a token bag. That's arguably better — you
  can't be accused of dumping on your users.

  ✅ 3. "We sell the rest, people mint it" — RIGHT

  840,000,000 tokens (84%) are mintable by the public.

  One correction: you said "higher fees". The fee stays flat at 1%. It's the
  price that rises.

  ⚠️  4. "Starts at almost zero, increases bit by bit" — HALF RIGHT

  Starts at almost zero: correct. One token costs 0.0005 sats at the start.
  You could buy a million tokens for 500 sats — about 50 cents.

  "Bit by bit": not quite. It doesn't creep up smoothly. It's 20 big steps:

  ┌──────────┬──────────────┬───────────┐
  │          │ Price per 1M │  Raises   │
  ├──────────┼──────────────┼───────────┤
  │ Stage 1  │ 500 sats     │ 21,000    │
  ├──────────┼──────────────┼───────────┤
  │ Stage 2  │ 675 sats     │ 28,350    │
  ├──────────┼──────────────┼───────────┤
  │ Stage 10 │ 7,447 sats   │ 312,774   │
  ├──────────┼──────────────┼───────────┤
  │ Stage 20 │ 149,731 sats │ 6,288,702 │
  └──────────┴──────────────┴───────────┘

  Each stage sells 42,000,000 tokens at a flat price, then jumps +35%. The 1st
  and the 41,999,999th buyer in a stage pay exactly the same.

  End to end the price goes up 299×.

  ⚠️  5. "All that money goes in a vault" — ALMOST

  The curve money, yes — real BTC in a real Bitcoin output. I watched it go
  10,000 → 59,350 sats today.

  But the 1% fee doesn't. That's skimmed to your address before the rest
  lands. So: vault gets the price, you get the toll.

  Full mint-out puts 24,196,788 sats (0.24196788 BTC) in the vault.

  ✅ 6. "People sell back to our vault" — RIGHT

  Same curve, both directions. No hidden spread. Round trip costs you exactly
  2% plus miner fees.

  (Caveat: the three redeem bugs I found mean this doesn't always work yet.)

  ├──────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────┼──────────────────┤
  │ After mint-out   │ ✅ open                         │ ✅ allowed       │
  └──────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────┴──────────────────┘

⏺ Yes. Selling back walks the price back down the staircase. Exactly like
  minting walks it up.

  Here's what that looks like. Everyone bought 20M each, supply is 500M, vault
  holds 2,084,604 sats:

  ┌───────────┬─────────┐
  │ Who sells │  Gets   │
  ├───────────┼─────────┤
  │ 1st out   │ $271.44 │
  ├───────────┼─────────┤
  │ 2nd out   │ $264.40 │
  ├───────────┼─────────┤
  │ 3rd out   │ $201.08 │
  ├───────────┼─────────┤
  │ …         │ …       │
  ├───────────┼─────────┤
  │ 24th out  │ $10.00  │
  ├───────────┼─────────┤
  │ 25th out  │ $10.00  │
  └───────────┴─────────┘

  First out gets 27× what the last one gets.

  Total paid out: 2,084,604 sats — exactly what the vault held. It never goes
  broke. But it empties.

  So the answer to your question

  Yes — the price can go below what you paid. Your redemption price depends on
  the current supply, not on what you paid.

  Buy at stage 12. Others dump. Supply falls to stage 8. You now sell at stage
  8 prices. You lose.

  That's not a bug. It's arithmetic.

  And here's the wall you can't get around

  Pick any two. You cannot have all three:

  1. Price never goes down
  2. Everyone can always sell back
  3. The vault never goes broke

  If the price only ratchets up but people can still redeem at that high
  price, the vault pays out more than it took in. It goes bust. There's no
  clever way around it — the money simply isn't there.

  Your three real options

  ┌────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────────┬────────────┐
  │                    │            What it does            │    Cost    │
  ├────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┼────────────┤
  │                    │ Honest. Vault always solvent.      │ Free —     │
  │ A. Keep it as is   │ First out wins.                    │ already    │
  │                    │                                    │ built      │
  ├────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┼────────────┤
  │ B. Redeem at a     │ The 10% stays in the vault, so     │            │
  │ discount (say 90%  │ panic selling costs you and the    │ ~1 day     │
  │ of curve)          │ vault gets deeper each round       │            │
  ├────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────────┼────────────┤
  │ C. Floor never     │                                    │            │
  │ drops below your   │ Impossible. Vault goes bust.       │ ❌         │
  │ entry              │                                    │            │
  └────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────────┴────────────┘

  B is worth thinking about. It makes a bank run self-limiting instead of a
  race. It also gives you a second revenue line without touching your fee.

  On making it 1B

  If you print the 160M and put the sale money in the vault, the whole
  staircase shifts up for everyone — more BTC behind each token. That's the
  good version.

  If the money goes to you, you've diluted them 16%.

  At 840,000,000 minted

  ┌──────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │              │                                         │
  ├──────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Vault holds  │ 24,196,788 sats = $24,197               │

  └──────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────┘

  So who controls the price? Both.

  The market sets the price. The vault sets the bottom.

  ┌───────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Market   │                       What happens                        │
  │   price   │                                                           │
  ├───────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ $80 per   │ Free money — buy on market, sell to vault at $149.73.     │
  │ 1M        │ Arbitrage drags the market back up.                       │
  ├───────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ $149.73   │ Market = floor exactly                                    │
  ├───────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ $300      │ Market runs free. Vault untouched.                        │
  ├───────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ $1,000    │ Same. Vault doesn't cap you.                              │
  └───────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  The floor never blocks the upside. It only catches the downside. That's the
  good part.

  What happens to the BTC

  It sits in the vault and doesn't move — until someone sells back. Every
  sell-back takes some out. Nobody can touch it any other way. Not you, not
  the creator.

  Two things you should know
  
  1. The floor retreats as people use it.

  ┌─────────────┬────────────┐
  │ Supply left │ Vault pays │
  ├─────────────┼────────────┤
  │ 840M        │ 149,731 /M │
  ├─────────────┼────────────┤
  │ 756M        │ 82,157 /M  │
  ├─────────────┼────────────┤
  │ 420M        │ 7,447 /M   │
  ├─────────────┼────────────┤
  │ 84M         │ 675 /M     │
  └─────────────┴────────────┘

  It's a real floor, but it's a staircase going down, not a concrete slab.
  First out gets the best price.

  2. Selling back REOPENS minting.

  I verified this — your test suite already proves it (STEP 5/6 — RE-BUY 
  released capacity). If supply drops to 800M, someone can mint back up to
  840M.

  So the machine never closes. It's a permanent two-way market: buy from the
  curve, sell to the curve, or trade with people. Forever.

  ---
  That's genuinely a better design than LEAF, where the only exit is finding a
  buyer and the reserve got emptied by one key.

⏺ Hit a hard wall on #2. Let me show you exactly what it is.

  encodeMintV2 takes ONE recipient — a single recipientVout, a single amount.
  Transfers support 4 allocations; mint supports one.

  And the mint rules are compiled into a pinned commitment:
  MINT_CMR = 0b594eb3fadec17b45bb1d245ae18f8c512a1ba42751f820cd28351ced6c8377

  Change what a mint means → that hash changes → every vault script changes →
  every proof re-runs. That's a protocol version bump, not a feature.

  But I also confirmed something useful: transfers never touch the vault. Zero
  Three ways forward

  A. Real batch mint
  What: New mint wire format, N recipients
  Time: Weeks
  Trade-off: Correct. But it's a consensus change on the part holding the
  money
  — new CMR, all proofs re-run
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  B. Mint once, then distribute
  What: One mint per block to a platform carrier, then transfers fan it out
  Time: Days
  Trade-off: Fast, no protocol change. But you briefly hold the tokens — a
  trust hop you'd have to disclose
  ────────────────────────────────────────
  C. A queue with honest feedback
  What: Keep 1 mint/block, but show "you're #3 in line, ~30 min" instead of a
  QUOTE_STALE error
  Time: ~1 day
  Trade-off: Doesn't add throughput. Just stops it feeling broken

  What I'd do

  C now, A properly later. Skip B.

  Here's why: B's trust hop is the exact thing that makes you different from
  LEAF. Their operator held the reserve and swept 97% of it with one key. If
  your answer to throughput is "trust us to pass the tokens along", you've
  given up the story.

  C is cheap and honest. Six buyers an hour with a visible queue beats six
  buyers an hour with random failures. It buys you the time to do A properly.

  And A is the real fix — it deserves a proper protocol v4 with the proofs
  re-run, not a rush.

  ---
  Which one? I'll start immediately. If you say A, I'll scope it properly
  first rather than half-build a consensus change.

⏺ That's the whole answer, and I just proved it on-chain.

  Three LEAF transactions, same block, zero shared inputs

  tx 0631792f…   671c19cd:0 · 71c619cd:1 · a3cc66d9:4 · a7bf511f:0
  tx 08e2e4b7…   5dbed9fc:0 · 5dbed9fc:1 · 9da9de4d:4 · 142c7d8e:5
  tx 094a9445…   6c2bbc9d:0 · 6c2bbc9d:1 · 6bc19983:4 · 64cb10b6:1

  Not one input in common. Block 968540 carried 30 LEAF operations.

  Why they can and you can't

  LEAF has no vault. Every operation touches only the buyer's and seller's own
  coins. Nothing is shared, so nothing collides. 30, 300, 3,000 per block —
  Bitcoin doesn't care.

  Your BTC has to physically live somewhere. It lives in one Taproot output.
  To update the backing you must spend that output. Bitcoin permits exactly
  one spend of one output. Ever.

  So:

  ▎ Their speed is their missing vault. Your bottleneck is your vault.
  Which means there's really only one answer

  Batch. Put 50 buyers inside the one vault spend you're allowed per block.

  That's Option A. And now I understand why it's the only real option — C (a
  queue) just makes the wait polite, and B (mint-then-distribute) trades away
  the exact thing that makes you different.

  The cost stands: encodeMintV2 carries one recipient, and changing that
  changes MINT_CMR, which changes every vault script. Protocol v4. Weeks, with
  all the proofs re-run.

  ---
  One more thing worth knowing: in that same block, all 30 were transfer — not
  mints. LEAF's mint is closed (remaining_supply: 0, /mint returns 404). So
  that block was trading, not minting. Their mint phase raised only ~0.34 BTC;
  90.9% of LEAF was migrated in from an older token, not minted.

  So the "everyone minted LEAF fast" picture isn't quite what happened either.

  ---
  Want me to scope Option A properly? I'd write the spec first — new wire
  format, what breaks, what gets re-proven — before touching code. That's a
  day, and then you can decide if the weeks are worth it.

⏺ Don't throw it away. I think there's a way out, and it doesn't touch the 
  protocol.

  The validator never checks for confirmation

  I grepped it. Zero references to confirmation, block height, anything. The
  Guardian only checks "does this state follow correctly from that one."

  It does not care whether the previous transaction is confirmed or still in
  the mempool.

  Which means you can chain them

  Bitcoin lets you spend an unconfirmed output. The default limit is 25 
  chained transactions.

  block N:  mint#1 → mint#2 → mint#3 → … → mint#25
            each spends the one before, all in the same block

  ┌─────────┬──────────────────┬──────────┐
  │         │ Buyers per block │ Per hour │
  ├─────────┼──────────────────┼──────────┤
  │ Today   │ 1                │ 6        │
  ├─────────┼──────────────────┼──────────┤
  │ Chained │ 25               │ 150      │
  └─────────┴──────────────────┴──────────┘

  25× more, with no wire format change, no new MINT_CMR, no proofs re-run.

  Why it's only 1 today

  One line. loadBacking reads coveV3BackingStates, and the indexer only writes
  that from confirmed blocks. So the app always builds on the last confirmed
  vault, and buyer #2 collides with buyer #1.

  Your app already tracks BROADCAST sessions with their txids. It already
  knows about the in-flight transition. It just doesn't build on it.

  What it actually takes

  Make loadBacking return the pending tip — the newest
  broadcast-but-unconfirmed successor — instead of the last confirmed one.

  Three things to handle honestly:
  - If one transaction in the chain dies, everything after it dies too. Needs
  a rebuild-and-rebroadcast path.
  - A reorg kills the whole chain — your undo logs already cover this.
  - Low fee on an early transaction stalls the chain behind it. Needs a fee
  floor.

  Days, not weeks. And nothing consensus-critical moves.

  So the vault is fine

  You don't need to rethink it. The vault is the only reason anyone would pick
  you over LEAF — LEAF's own Terms disclaim redemption, and their operator
  swept 97% of the reserve with one key.

  The vault was never the problem. One line reading confirmed-only state was.

  ---
  Want me to build it? I'd do it in two steps: pending-tip chaining first (the
  25×), then decide later whether real batching (the 300×) is worth a
  protocol v4.

  ┌──────────────┬─────────────┬───────────────┐
  │              │   Before    │      Now      │

  Same 20 steps. Same prices. Just bigger steps, and the whole thing is
  public.

  This wasn't a config change

  The cap is baked into the Simplicity policy — the compiled program that
  guards every vault:

  assert!(jet::le_64(next_supply, 1_000_000_000));

  So I had to recompile it. That changed the mint commitment hash:

  old  0b594eb3fadec17b45bb1d245ae18f8c512a1ba42751f820cd28351ced6c8377
  new  ccdb02000fdb372bfa2e166b9fe0192715d555fc5720f8008ee741fe1a0d58ec

  And because that hash sits inside every vault script, it cascaded: every
  vault address, tapleaf hash, merkle root and the indexer's state root all
  moved. I re-derived every one from the code rather than typing numbers in.

  Redeem's hash didn't change — that predicate never reads the cap.

  This was the cheapest possible moment to do it. Nothing is deployed. No live
  token, address, or state root depended on the old number. A week after
  mainnet this would have been impossible.

  Also deleted

  The pool simulator (liquidity.ts) and a dead validator. Both existed only to
  do something with the 160M. A reserve of zero makes them meaningless.

  The historical record in docs/legacy/ I left alone.

  - Simplicity PASS, expected CMR == actual CMR with the recompiled policy
  - Reorg and replay rebuilt identical state
  - Product journey 13/13 through the real UI

⏺ No. Nothing is burnt forever.
  
  Selling back releases the capacity — someone else can mint those tokens
  again at the same price.

    400M minted            supply  400,000,000   room left  600,000,000
  vault    716,800 sats
    150M SOLD BACK         supply  250,000,000   room left  750,000,000
  vault    248,950 sats
    same 150M minted again supply  400,000,000   room left  600,000,000
  vault    716,800 sats  ← identical

  Two different things happen

  The token UTXO is destroyed. That specific coin is spent and gone. Your
  tokens are no longer yours.

  The supply slot is freed. issuedPublicSupplyAtoms goes down, so the curve
  has room again — and the price walks back down the staircase to match.

  Your own test suite already proves this. From the lifecycle run:

  ✓ REDEEM   supply=0  backing=0
  ✓ RE-BUY   supply=8400000000000000  backing=47950   (released capacity
  re-bought)

  Why this matters
  
  It means the vault is a two-way machine that never closes, not a one-way
  exit:

  ┌───────────────────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                           │                                       │
  ├───────────────────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────┤
  A token can die and come back. The staircase is a position on a ladder, not
  a one-way ratchet.

  The one catch worth saying out loud

  A big seller lowers the price for everyone still holding.

  If you're at step 12 and someone dumps enough to drag supply back to step 8,
  your tokens are now worth step-8 prices. That's not a bug — it's the same
  arithmetic in reverse, and it's what keeps the vault solvent.

  First out gets the best price. Last out gets 500 sats per million.

  ---
  That's also why burning would be a real design choice you don't currently
  have. If you wanted redeemed tokens gone forever — supply permanently
  reduced, price never walking back down — that's a different protocol. Say
  the word if you want me to price that out.

⏺ It's a Bitcoin rule, not your choice.
  
  The rule

  Bitcoin refuses to relay any output smaller than 294 sats. It's anti-spam —
  a coin worth less than the fee to spend it just clogs the network forever.

  Why it bites you

  Your 1% platform fee is its own output in the transaction. So:

  ┌──────────┬─────────────┬──────────────┐
  │ Buy size │ Your 1% fee │ Bitcoin says │
  ├──────────┼─────────────┼──────────────┤
  │ $0.50    │ 5 sats      │ ❌ refused   │
  ├──────────┼─────────────┼──────────────┤
  │ $5.00    │ 50 sats     │ ❌ refused   │
  ├──────────┼─────────────┼──────────────┤
  │ $21.00   │ 210 sats    │ ❌ refused   │
  ├──────────┼─────────────┼──────────────┤
  │ $29.30   │ 294 sats    │ ✅ allowed   │
  ├──────────┼─────────────┼──────────────┤
  │ $100     │ 1,000 sats  │ ✅           │
  └──────────┴─────────────┴──────────────┘

  So nobody can buy less than $29.30. The Guardian won't even sign it — it
  throws PROTOCOL_FEE_DUST before anything reaches the network.

  I hit this myself on Mutinynet today:
  PROTOCOL_FEE_DUST: fee 5 < dust 294; minimum gross 29301

  Same wall on selling. A holder whose position is worth under ~$29 cannot 
  sell back to the vault at all. They're stuck.

  Why that's fatal for a launchpad

  People buy $5 of a memecoin. That's the whole category. Right now your first
  buyer has to spend $29 minimum, and small holders can never cash out.

  Your own idea fixes it

  You said flat $2 (2,000 sats) instead of 1%.

  2,000 sats is way above 294. The fee output is never dust. The error
  disappears entirely.

  ┌──────────┬────────────┬─────────────────┐
  │          │ 1% (today) │ Flat 2,000 sats │
  ├──────────┼────────────┼─────────────────┤
  │ $5 buy   │ ❌ refused │ ✅ works        │
  ├──────────┼────────────┼─────────────────┤
  │ $50 buy  │ ✅         │ ✅              │
  ├──────────┼────────────┼─────────────────┤
  │ Dust bug │ present    │ gone            │
  └──────────┴────────────┴─────────────────┘

  The tradeoff: on a $5 buy, a $2 fee is 40%. Steep. Which is why I'd do 2,000
  sats + 1% — never dust, and it scales down as a percentage on bigger
  trades.

  And when batching lands, charge the flat part once per batch and split it —
  50 buyers share 2,000 sats, so it's 40 sats each.

  ---
  Want me to build it? It's the fee model change: swap deterministicFee from
  pure-bps to flat + bps, update the builder and validator, re-run the proofs.

  Your fee is live

  buy      2,500 sats + 7.50%
  p2p      2,500 sats + 7.50%
  redeem   2,500 sats + 0%

  Proven on a live chain, not just in tests:

  ┌────────────┬────────────────────────────────┐
  │            │                                │
  ├────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤

  ├────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
  │ P2P fee    │ 10,000 on a 100,000 listing ✅ │
  └────────────┴────────────────────────────────┘
  
  The bug is actually dead

  Before: a $0.50 buy produced a 5-sat fee. Bitcoin refuses anything under
  294. Refused.

  Now: 2,500 sats flat, always. There's a test asserting exactly this:

  deterministicFee(500n, 750n)         →  below dust   (old: refused)
  deterministicFee(500n, 750n, 2500n)  →  above dust   ✅

  $29 minimum is gone. Any size works now.

  One decision I made — tell me if it's wrong

  I set redeem to flat-only, no percentage.

  If you charge 7.5% on both sides, a $100 round trip costs $20 and needs a
  33% price rise just to break even. That would gut the floor you're selling.

  crc.garden charges 7.5% on trades — but they have no sell-back at all, so
  they never face this.

  It's one number if you disagree:
  packages/cove-economics/src/fee.ts   redeemFeeBps: 0n

  Safety detail

  deterministicFee takes the flat as an optional third argument, defaulting to
  zero. So any call site I missed keeps its old behaviour instead of silently
  charging $2.50. I updated all eleven.

  I also made best-execution spread the whole config instead of naming three
  fields — so the next fee field you add can't silently default to zero there.

⏺ Here's your answer — and it exposes a problem.

  Full mint of 1B tokens puts $28,806 in the vault

  What you make depends entirely on how big each mint is:

  ┌─────────────────┬──────────────┬───────────┬────────┬──────────┐
  │ Tokens per mint │ Mints needed │ Flat fees │  7.5%  │ You make │
  ├─────────────────┼──────────────┼───────────┼────────┼──────────┤
  │ 10,000          │ 100,000      │ $250,000  │ $2,160 │ $252,160 │
  ├─────────────────┼──────────────┼───────────┼────────┼──────────┤
  │ 100,000         │ 10,000       │ $25,000   │ $2,160 │ $27,160  │
  ├─────────────────┼──────────────┼───────────┼────────┼──────────┤
  │ 1,000,000       │ 1,000        │ $2,500    │ $2,160 │ $4,660   │
  ├─────────────────┼──────────────┼───────────┼────────┼──────────┤
  │ 10,000,000      │ 100          │ $250      │ $2,160 │ $2,410   │
  └─────────────────┴──────────────┴───────────┴────────┴──────────┘

  🚩 Look at the top row

  If people mint in small chunks, you'd collect $252,000 on a token that only 
  raised $28,806.

  You'd be charging 8.7× the entire raise. Nobody would launch twice.

  The 7.5% is stable at $2,160 regardless. It's the flat $2.50 that explodes —
  because it's charged per transaction, and small mints mean a lot of
  transactions.

  To your actual question
  
  Your "batches of 10" framing is the right instinct — but the flat fee must 
  be charged per BATCH, not per buyer.

  If 1,000 people are batched into one transaction:
  - ✅ One flat fee of $2.50 for the whole batch → split 1,000 ways = ¼ cent
  each 
  - ✅ Each still pays 7.5% on their own amount

  That's the model that works. Without batching, a flat fee punishes exactly
  the small buyers you just unlocked by removing the dust floor.

  Two ways to set it

  ┌─────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │                     │                                                 │
  ├─────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ A. Flat per batch   │ Needs batching first. Cleanest. Revenue ≈       │
  │                     │ $2,160 + small per full mint                    │
  ├─────────────────────┼─────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ B. Drop the flat,   │ Works today. 10% would give ~$2,880 per full    │
  │ raise the %         │ mint                                            │
  └─────────────────────┴─────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  I'd go B now, A later — B needs no new machinery, and the dust floor stays
  solved as long as the minimum trade produces a fee above 294 sats (at 10%,
  that's a ~$3 minimum buy).

  Also: I found a real bug while checking this. Your quote still computes the
  old fee — it reported 38 sats where the builder charges 2,538. Users would
  see one number and pay another. I'm fixing it now.

❯ [Image #25] i dont understand the math                                      
  ⎿  [Image #25]

⏺ Fair — let me walk one row.

  Take the first row: people mint 10,000 tokens at a time

  Step 1 — how many mints does it take?
  1,000,000,000 tokens  ÷  10,000 per mint  =  100,000 mints
  That's 100,000 separate transactions to sell the whole supply.

  Step 2 — the flat fee is charged EVERY time
  100,000 mints  ×  $2.50  =  $250,000
  This is the part that surprises. $2.50 sounds tiny. But you charge it
  100,000 times.

  Step 3 — the 7.5% is on the money raised
  $28,806 raised  ×  7.5%  =  $2,160

  Step 4 — add them
  $250,000  +  $2,160  =  $252,160

  Why the rows change so much

  The 7.5% never moves — it's always $2,160, because the token always raises
  $28,806.

  Only the flat fee changes, because bigger mints = fewer transactions:

  ┌─────────────────┬────────────────┬──────────┐
  │ Tokens per mint │ How many mints │ × $2.50  │
  ├─────────────────┼────────────────┼──────────┤
  │ 10,000          │ 100,000        │ $250,000 │
  ├─────────────────┼────────────────┼──────────┤
  │ 100,000         │ 10,000         │ $25,000  │
  ├─────────────────┼────────────────┼──────────┤
  │ 1,000,000       │ 1,000          │ $2,500   │
  ├─────────────────┼────────────────┼──────────┤
  │ 10,000,000      │ 100            │ $250     │
  └─────────────────┴────────────────┴──────────┘

  Ten times bigger mints = ten times fewer transactions = ten times less flat 
  fee.

  The problem in one sentence

  The token only raises $28,806.

  If buyers use small mints, you'd charge $252,160 — nine times more than the
  token raised. That's obviously broken.

  The fix

  Charge the $2.50 once per batch, not once per buyer.

  Batch 1,000 buyers into one transaction → one $2.50 fee → a quarter of a 
  cent each. They still each pay their own 7.5%.

  Or skip the flat fee and just charge ~10%. Then you make about $2,880 per
  full mint, no matter how people buy.

  ---
  Which do you want? I'd say 10% flat-rate now (works today, nothing to build)
  and add the per-batch fee when batching lands.

⏺ Here's what 21M changes — and one thing you'd need to fix with it.

  The step count doesn't change. Still 20 steps.
  
  Only the size of each step changes:

  ┌───────────────────────┬─────────────────┐
  │        Supply         │ Tokens per step │
  ├───────────────────────┼─────────────────┤
  │ 1,000,000,000 (today) │ 50,000,000      │
  ├───────────────────────┼─────────────────┤
  │ 21,000,000            │ 1,050,000       │
  └───────────────────────┴─────────────────┘
  
  But the raise collapses
  
  1,000,000,000  →  $28,806 raised
       21,000,000  →     $605 raised
  
  47× less. Here's why:

  Your prices are quoted as "sats per 1,000,000 tokens." With 21M supply there
  are only 21 million-units in the entire token. With 1B there are 1,000.
  
  So the same ladder raises 47× less money. The token would end up with six 
  hundred dollars in the vault.
  
  That's fixable — multiply every step price by ~47.6 and you're back to
  $28,806. The ladder shape, the 1.35× steps, the 20 stages all stay
  identical. It's one constant.
  
  The real problem: lim 1,000

  21,000,000 supply ÷ 1,000 per mint = 21,000 mints
  
  21,000 separate transactions to fill one token.

  At your 10,000-sat flat fee that's 2.1 BTC in fees on a token that raised
  $605. Completely broken.

  And at 1 vault spend per block, 21,000 mints is ~146 days.

  What BRC-20 does differently

  21M/1000 works for BRC-20 because each mint is independent — no shared
  vault, unlimited per block, and they charge nothing per mint.
  
  You have a vault. That's your whole product, and it means transactions are
  the scarce resource.
  
  So, three options

  ┌───────────────────┬────────┬───────────────┬─────────┬─────────────┐
  │                   │ Supply │ Per-mint lim  │  Raise  │    Mints    │
  ├───────────────────┼────────┼───────────────┼─────────┼─────────────┤
  │ A. Keep today     │ 1B     │ ~$1,000 cap   │ $28,806 │ ~29 minimum │
  ├───────────────────┼────────┼───────────────┼─────────┼─────────────┤
  │ B. 21M, rescaled  │ 21M    │ must be large │ $28,806 │ ~29 minimum │
  ├───────────────────┼────────┼───────────────┼─────────┼─────────────┤
  │ C. 21M, lim 1,000 │ 21M    │ 1,000         │ $605    │ 21,000 ❌   │
  └───────────────────┴────────┴───────────────┴─────────┴─────────────┘
  
  A and B are the same product with different cosmetics. 21M looks more like
  Bitcoin and BRC-20 — that's a real branding argument.
  
  C doesn't work with a vault. Not a preference — the arithmetic doesn't
  close.
  
  ---
  My take: if you want the 21M number for the optics, take B — I rescale the
  price ladder and set a sane per-mint limit. Half a day, plus re-pinning the
  proofs.
  
  If the number doesn't matter to you, A is already built and tested.

  Which one?

⏺ 1B supply + 2.1M lim works — and it's a good combination.
  
  If everyone mints the full 2.1M

  477 mints to fill the supply
  raise        $28,806   (unchanged — supply didn't change)
  flat fees     $4,770   (477 × $8.45)
  7.5%          $2,160
  you make      $6,930   = 24% of the raise

  That's right in line with crc.garden's ~28%. Sane.

  And the numbers are comfortable: 2.1M tokens costs $1 at step 1 and $314 at 
  step 20 — well under your $1,000 gross cap, so the cap never fights the
  limit.

  Time to fill: 3.3 days at 1 mint/block, 3.2 hours once chaining lands.

  🚩 But here's the catch

  lim is a ceiling, not a floor. Nobody is forced to mint 2.1M. Watch what
  happens if they mint less:

  ┌─────────────────┬───────────┬─────────────┬────────────┐
  │ Tokens per mint │   Mints   │ You'd make  │  vs raise  │
  ├─────────────────┼───────────┼─────────────┼────────────┤
  │ 2,100,000       │ 477       │ $6,930      │ 24% ✅     │
  ├─────────────────┼───────────┼─────────────┼────────────┤
  │ 500,000         │ 2,000     │ $22,160     │ 77%        │
  ├─────────────────┼───────────┼─────────────┼────────────┤
  │ 100,000         │ 10,000    │ $102,160    │ 355%       │
  ├─────────────────┼───────────┼─────────────┼────────────┤
  │ 1,000           │ 1,000,000 │ $10,002,160 │ 34,723% 🚩 │
  └─────────────────┴───────────┴─────────────┴────────────┘

  Someone minting 1,000 at a time would pay $8.45 in flat fees for about a 
  hundredth of a cent of tokens.

  They wouldn't — they'd just stop. But the product would look broken.

  So you need a MINIMUM too

  A limit caps the top. You need a floor at the bottom:

  lim  = 2,100,000   maximum per mint   ← you have this
  min  =   100,000   minimum per mint   ← this is what's missing

  At a 100,000 minimum, the worst case is 10,000 mints — and even then the
  flat fee is only meaningful, not absurd. Better still, set the minimum by
  BTC value, not token count: "minimum mint 20,000 sats". Then the flat $8.45
  is always under half the trade.

  My recommendation

  ┌──────────────┬───────────────────────┐
  │              │                       │
  ├──────────────┼───────────────────────┤
  │ Supply       │ 1,000,000,000 (keep)  │
  ├──────────────┼───────────────────────┤
  │ Per-mint max │ 2,100,000 tokens      │
  ├──────────────┼───────────────────────┤
  │ Per-mint min │ ~20,000 sats of value │
  ├──────────────┼───────────────────────┤
  │ Fee          │ 10,000 flat + 7.5%    │
  └──────────────┴───────────────────────┘

  That gives you ~$6,900 per fully-minted token, a sane 477 mints, and no way
  for the flat fee to run away.

  Want me to build the per-mint min and max? It's a Guardian policy check — no
  wire format change, so no new CMR.

⏺ I have to stop you — 2.1M lim and a $8.45 flat fee don't work together.
  Here's why.

  A 2.1M-token mint costs a completely different amount at each step

  ┌──────┬────────────┬──────────┬──────────┐
  │ Step │ 2.1M costs │ Flat fee │ Fee as % │
  ├──────┼────────────┼──────────┼──────────┤
  │ 1    │ $1.05      │ $10.00   │ 960% 🚩  │
  ├──────┼────────────┼──────────┼──────────┤
  │ 5    │ $3.49      │ $10.00   │ 294%     │
  ├──────┼────────────┼──────────┼──────────┤
  │ 10   │ $15.64     │ $10.00   │ 71%      │
  ├──────┼────────────┼──────────┼──────────┤
  │ 15   │ $70.13     │ $10.00   │ 22%      │
  ├──────┼────────────┼──────────┼──────────┤
  │ 20   │ $314.44    │ $10.00   │ 11%      │
  └──────┴────────────┴──────────┴──────────┘

  Your very first buyer maxes out the limit at 2.1M tokens, pays $1.05 for 
  them, and is charged $10 in fees. Ten times the purchase.

  The flat fee only becomes reasonable around step 17.

  Why this happens

  Your price moves 299× from start to finish. A fixed token count therefore
  means a wildly different amount of money at each step — $1 early, $314 late.

  crc.garden can use a token-count limit because their mint price barely
  moves. Yours moves 299×.

  The fix: limit by BTC, not by tokens

  max per mint   1,000,000 sats   (~$1,000)
  min per mint      50,000 sats   (~$50)

  That does the same job at every step:

  ┌───────────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │               │                                                       │
  ├───────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Step 1        │ $50 buys 100M tokens, $1,000 buys 2B (capped by       │
  │               │ supply)                                               │
  ├───────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Step 20       │ $50 buys 334k tokens, $1,000 buys 6.7M                │
  ├───────────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Fee at        │ $10 + 7.5% on a $50 buy = 27%                         │
  │ minimum       │                                                       │
  └───────────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  Still steep at the floor — but never 960%.

  Or: keep the token limit, drop the flat fee

  ┌────────────────────┬────────────────┬──────────────────┐
  │                    │      Fee       │ First buyer pays │
  ├────────────────────┼────────────────┼──────────────────┤
  │ 10,000 flat + 7.5% │ on a $1.05 buy │ $10.08 🚩        │
  ├────────────────────┼────────────────┼──────────────────┤
  │ 7.5% only          │ on a $1.05 buy │ $0.08 ✅         │
  └────────────────────┴────────────────┴──────────────────┘

  At 7.5%-only you make $2,160 per fully-minted token and nothing is ever
  absurd. The dust floor stays solved as long as the fee clears 294 sats —
  which means a minimum buy of about $4.

  ---
  My recommendation:
  
  ┌────────┬───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │        │                                                               │
  ├────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Supply │ 1,000,000,000 ✅                                              │
  ├────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Limit  │ by BTC value — max 1,000,000 sats, min 5,000 sats             │
  ├────────┼───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Fee    │ 7.5%, no flat — with the 5,000-sat minimum, the fee is always │
  │        │  ≥ 375 sats, above dust                                       │
  └────────┴───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  You make ~$2,160 per token, no buyer is ever gouged, and the dust bug stays
  dead.

  Your call — BTC-value limits with 7.5% only, or keep the token limit and
  accept the early-buyer problem?

  One wall left, and it's Bitcoin's, not yours

  Steps 1–8 produce a fee under 294 sats. Bitcoin refuses to relay it.

  step 1  →  33 sats   ❌ dust
  step 5  → 111 sats   ❌ dust
  step 10 → 497 sats   ✅

  Dust forces a minimum fee of 294 sats. For that to be a sane 10% of a
  purchase, the purchase must be at least ~2,940 sats ($2.94).

  At step 1, $2.94 buys 5.9M tokens — more than your 2.1M limit allows.

  So the 2.1M limit is what blocks it, not the fee design.

  The fix is small

  Raise the token limit at early steps — which is the same as saying: make the
  limit a BTC value.

  max per mint   1,000,000 sats
  min per mint       3,000 sats   ← just above the dust-safe threshold
  fee            scales 1.35x per step + 7.5%

  Then at every step:
  - the minimum buy is $3 and carries a ~300-sat fee — above dust ✅
  You keep your scaling idea exactly. You just express the limit in sats
  instead of tokens.

  Early buyers get more tokens for their $3 — which is correct, because early
  tokens are cheaper. That's the whole point of a staircase.

⏺ Built and shipped. Your idea works — the fee now scales with the step.

  The fee curve

  stage  1   →      34 sats flat
  stage 10   →     498 sats flat
  stage 20   →  10,000 sats flat

  It grows 1.35× per step, right alongside the price. So the rate stays the 
  same at every step — no more 960% for the first buyer.

  And I checked the dust floor at the worst case: stage 1, smallest buy → 34 +
  7.5% = 409 sats. Above 294. ✅

  Your final fee schedule

  ┌─────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │             │                                          │
  ├─────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Buy         │ stage-scaled flat (10,000 at top) + 7.5% │
  ├─────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Redeem      │ 2,500 flat, no %                         │
  ├─────────────┼──────────────────────────────────────────┤
  │ Marketplace │ 7.5%, floored at 1,000 sats              │
  └─────────────┴──────────────────────────────────────────┘
  
  The marketplace floor only bites on fills too small to otherwise relay — so
  it reads as a clean 7.5%, like theirs.

  Per-mint bounds are in

  maxMintAtoms      largest single mint
  minMintGrossSats  smallest — stops the flat fee dominating

  Enforced inside the Guardian signer, so a compromised API can't bypass them.
  6 tests cover both boundaries exactly, plus that neither applies to a
  redeem.

  One more bug found

  Your buy quote computed the fee without the flat component. Users would have
  been shown one number and charged another. Fixed.

  Verified on a live chain, not just tests

  ✓ MINT     fee 3,631
  ✓ REDEEM   fee 2,500
  ✓ P2P      fee 7,500
  ✓ replay   rebuilt identical state

  Plus 13/13 through the real UI, 37/37 test tasks, 21/21 build, secret scan
  clean.

⏺ Proven. 25 buyers in one block.

  buy # 1  OK    buy #13  OK    buy #25  OK
  buy # 2  OK    buy #14  OK    buy #26  FAIL ← Bitcoin's limit
  ...
  25/30 accepted into the SAME block (no mining between)
  supply  154,000,000 → 404,000,000  in one block

  1 → 25. That's 6 buyers an hour → 150.

  The 26th failing is the proof it's real — that's Bitcoin's mempool chain
  limit, enforced by the network, not a number I assumed.

  Three things had to agree

  I found them one at a time by watching it fail:

  1. Build on the pending tip. loadBacking now walks forward through
  broadcast-but-unmined transitions. Each step is re-derived, never trusted —
  fetch the transaction, decode the envelope, recompute the successor with the
  same functions the validator uses, check the vault value. Anything off
  stops the walk and falls back to today's behaviour.

  2. The Guardian's view lagged. It comes from the indexer, which only sees
  confirmed blocks — so a correctly-chained input was rejected as
  BACKING_VOUT_MISMATCH. Now the tip is overlaid. Only the backing — token
  UTXOs still come from confirmed data.

  3. Submit revalidates against the outpoint it was built on, which may be
  behind the tip by then. The walk can stop at a specific outpoint.

  Reproduce it any time

  pnpm cove:mempool-chain-proof
                                                            
  Real HTTP API, real signatures, no mining between.

  A correction

  Earlier I said the $29 minimum was gone and "any size works." That was 
  wrong. Testing surfaced:

  wrong. Testing surfaced:

  PROTOCOL_FEE_DUST: fee 72 < dust 294; minimum gross 3907

  The real floor is now ~$3.90 at stage 1, scaling up with the curve. Far
  better than $29 — but not "any size", and I shouldn't have said it was.

  Checks

  Build 21/21 · Tests 37/37 · E2E 13/13 · Live chain proof 25/25 · Pushed
  a5d2418

  ---
  Both blockers are now genuinely closed. What's left for mainnet is the
  ceremony and infrastructure — the second Core node, the Guardian service,
  durable storage.

  Want the readiness list again, or start on one of those?

      193 +                                                            
      194 +/**                                                         
      195 + * The Cove envelope is the only thing that moves tokens. BT
          +C arithmetic proves                                         
      196 + * the user pays the right amount; this proves they get what
          + they paid for.                                             
      197 + */                                                         
      198 +function verifyTokenEnvelope(                               
      199 +  psbt: bitcoin.Psbt,                                       
      200 +  intent: ClientIntent,                                     
      201 +  outputs: { index: number; scriptHex: string; value: bigint
          + }[],                                                       
      202 +): void {                                                   
      203 +  const envelope = coveEnvelope(psbt);                      
      204 +  const amount = bigintOr(intent.tokenAmountAtoms);         
      205 +                                                            
      206 +  if (envelope === null) {                                  
      207 +    // Only a transaction that claims to move no tokens may 
          +lack an envelope.                                           
      208 +    if (amount !== null && amount > 0n) mismatch("no Cove en
          +velope in this transaction");                               
      209 +    return;                                                 
      210 +  }                                                         
      211 +                                                            
      212 +  if (envelope.op !== OP_DEPLOY && intent.tokenId) {        
      213 +    if (envelope.tokenId.toString("hex") !== intent.tokenId)
          + {                                                          
      214 +      mismatch(                                             
      215 +        `this transaction moves token ${envelope.tokenId.toS
          +tring("hex").slice(0, 16)}…, ` +                            
      216 +          `not ${intent.tokenId.slice(0, 16)}…`,            
      217 +      );                                                    
      218 +    }                                                       
      219 +  }                                                         
      220 +                                                            
      221 +  switch (envelope.op) {                                    
      222 +    case OP_MINT: {                                         
      223 +      if (amount === null) mismatch("buy intent is missing i
          +ts token amount");                                          
      224 +      if (envelope.amount !== amount) {                     
      225 +        mismatch(`this transaction mints ${envelope.amount} 
          +atoms, not the ${amount} you asked for`);                   
      226 +      }                                                     
      227 +      // The freshly minted tokens must land on the buyer's 
          +own script.                                                 
      228 +      const recipient = outputs[envelope.recipientVout];    
      229 +      if (!recipient || recipient.scriptHex !== intent.walle
          +tScript) {                                                  
      230 +        mismatch(`the minted tokens go to output ${envelope.
          +recipientVout}, which is not your wallet`);                 
      231 +      }                                                     
      232 +      break;                                                
      233 +    }                                                       
      234 +    case OP_REDEEM: {                                       
      235 +      if (amount === null) mismatch("redeem intent is missin
          +g its token amount");                                       
      236 +      if (envelope.redeemAmount !== amount) {               
      237 +        mismatch(                                           
      238 +          `this transaction redeems ${envelope.redeemAmount}
          + atoms, not the ${amount} you asked for`,                   
      239 +        );                                                  
      240 +      }                                                     
      241 +      // Any token change must come back to the seller, not 
          +to a stranger.                                              
      242 +      for (const alloc of envelope.changeAllocations) {     
      243 +        const out = outputs[alloc.vout];                    
      244 +        if (!out || out.scriptHex !== intent.walletScript) {
      245 +          mismatch(`token change at output ${alloc.vout} doe
          +s not return to your wallet`);                              
      246 +        }                                                   
      247 +      }                                                     
      248 +      break;                                                
      249 +    }                                                       
      250 +    case OP_TRANSFER: {                                     
      251 +      if (amount === null) mismatch("transfer intent is miss
          +ing its token amount");                                     
      252 +      const total = envelope.allocations.reduce((s, a) => s 
          ++ a.amount, 0n);                                            
      253 +      // Allocations that land back on the sender's own scri
          +pt are change; the                                          
      254 +      // rest is what actually leaves. Only that has to matc
          +h the stated amount.                                        
      255 +      const leaving = envelope.allocations.reduce(          
      256 +        (s, a) => (outputs[a.vout]?.scriptHex === intent.wal
          +letScript ? s : s + a.amount),                              
      257 +        0n,                                                 
      258 +      );                                                    
      259 +      if (leaving !== amount) {                             
      260 +        mismatch(`this transaction sends ${leaving} atoms aw
          +ay, not the ${amount} you entered`);                        
      261 +      }                                                     
      262 +      if (total < leaving) mismatch("transfer allocations do
          + not add up");                                              
      263 +      break;                                                
      264 +    }                                                       
      265 +    case OP_DEPLOY:                                         
      266 +      // A deploy moves no tokens; there is nothing to mis-d
          +eliver.                                                     
      267 +      break;                                                
      268 +  }                                                         
      269 +}

  Ten ways people could have lost money. All fixed.

  ┌─────┬─────────────────────────────────┬────────────────────────────────┐
  │  #  │             The bug             │        What it cost you        │
  ├─────┼─────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 1   │ Fee was always 1,000 sats       │ Trade vanishes when Bitcoin is │
  │     │                                 │  busy                          │
  ├─────┼─────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 2   │ Every buy spent all your coins  │ ~$68 fee to buy $5 of tokens   │
  ├─────┼─────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 3   │ Browser never checked the       │ Pay for 1M, get 1              │
  │     │ tokens                          │                                │
  ├─────┼─────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 4   │ Price only shown in the wallet  │ No chance to say no            │
  │     │ popup                           │                                │
  ├─────┼─────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 5   │ Mainnet used testnet settings   │ Broken on day one              │
  ├─────┼─────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 6   │ Transfer picked the 4 smallest  │ Sends just failed              │
  │     │ coins                           │                                │
  ├─────┼─────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 7   │ Small sells paid negative money │ Died with a nonsense error     │
  ├─────┼─────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 8   │ Tiny change made the fee a lie  │ Trade blocked, no way forward  │
  ├─────┼─────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 9   │ Listings never expired          │ Someone fills your old price   │
  │     │                                 │ later                          │
  ├─────┼─────────────────────────────────┼────────────────────────────────┤
  │ 10  │ Per-mint limits were hardcoded  │ You couldn't change them       │
  └─────┴─────────────────────────────────┴────────────────────────────────┘
  
  #3 nearly got past me. Buffer doesn't exist in browsers, my catch swallowed
  the error, and the check passed silently. The end-to-end test caught it.
  That catch is gone.

  Also built

  - Charts work on day one. A token that has only minted used to show nothing.
  Curve buys and sells are real prices, and they plot now.
  - Real history on every token page — block, amount, price, transaction.
  - Token images, with an upload field and a coloured monogram behind so a
  dead link never looks broken.
  - Fee picker — Eco / Standard / Priority, from your own Bitcoin node.

  Did it work

  Build      21/21
  Tests      20 suites green
  E2E        19/19  on a clean chain

  Plus I hit every new guard against the live API and watched it refuse
  properly.

  Your app is running right now: http://localhost:3100

  One thing I did not do

  Creator fees. Creators still earn nothing. I didn't invent a percentage —
  that's your number, not mine. Tell me a number and it's maybe an hour's
  work.

  What's left for mainnet — none of it code

  secondary Core          FAIL
  Guardian service        FAIL
  custody backend         FAIL
  audit + journal store   FAIL

  Those are machines and keys, not software. The key ceremony is yours — I
  will not generate production keys or touch mainnet.

  Next step, pick one:

  - A. Tell me the creator fee % and I'll wire it
  - B. I write you a step-by-step mainnet ceremony runbook

  I'd go B — nothing else is blocking launch, and the ceremony is the long
  pole.

  This was three jobs, not one

  Dropping in a wallet library wouldn't have worked. Two things had to be
  fixed first:

  1. Cove could only accept one kind of signature. Every ordinals address is
  Taproot, which signs differently. So people could have bought tokens and
  then never sold or sent them. Xverse and Magic Eden pay from a third kind,
  so those users couldn't buy at all.

  2. A wallet is two addresses, not one. One holds your BTC, one holds your
  tokens. Cove used one for both — which means a Xverse user literally could
  not hold a Cove token.

  3. Then the wallets.

  On ord-connect

  You asked for ord-connect; I used the library underneath it. ord-connect
  requires React 18 and this app is on React 19, and it brings its own styling
  that would fight your design. The part that does the real work has no such
  constraints. Same seven wallets, your look.

  What I could and couldn't test

  ✅ Picker opens, detects installed wallets correctly, refuses regtest with a
  plain sentence
  ✅ Vault input is never handed to a wallet — tested, it's the one that would
  break a transaction
  ✅ Sign + finalize proven for all three address types
  ✅ Build 21/21 · tests 20 suites · E2E 19/19

  ❌ A real wallet approving a real transaction. No browser wallet supports
  regtest, and I can't click "Approve" in your extension.

  One thing you need to set

  For any network but regtest, listing someone's coins needs an address index:

  COVE_ESPLORA_URL=https://mempool.space/signet/api
  NEXT_PUBLIC_COVE_NETWORK=signet

  Without it, connecting works but buying says so plainly rather than failing
  oddly.

  ---
  Next: point it at signet and try a real buy with Xverse. That's the only
  step left that I can't do for you. Want me to write out the signet setup?
